speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INVASION OF WESTERN EUROPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at half-past three o'clock this morning the government received by radio the following communique from General Eisenhower's headquarters:
Under the command of General Eisenhower, allied naval forces, supported by strong air forces, began landing of allied, armies this morning on the northern coast of France.
Ten minutes later from General Eisenhower's headquarters the following bulletin was received:
It is announced that General Bernard Montgomery is in command of the army group carrying out the assault. This army group includes British, Canadian and American forces.
At eight o'clock this morning I made the following radio broadcast:
"At half-past three o'clock this morning the government received official word that the invasion of western Europe had begun. Word was also received that Canadian troops were among the allied forces who landed this morning on the northern coast of France. Canada will be proud to learn that our troops are being supported by units of the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Air Force. The great landing in western Europe is the opening up of what we hope and believe will be the decisive phase of the war against Germany. The fighting is certain to be heavy, bitter and costly. We must not expect early results. We should be prepared for local reverses as well as successes. No one can say how long this phase of the war may last, but we have every reason for confidence in the final outcome.
" I cannot better express to the people of Canada the government's feelings at this moment than by giving to you the words of General Crerar, the Canadian army commander, as conveyed to the Canadian assault forces on the eve of their embarkation:
" ' I have,' said General Crerar, ' complete confidence in our ability to meet the tests which lie ahead. We are excellently trained and equipped. The quality of both the senior and junior leadership is of the highest. As Canadians, we inherit military characteristics which were feared by the enemy in the last great war. Thev will be still more feared before this war terminates.'
"I should like to add this word: Let the hearts of all in Canada to-day be filled with
(Mr. Pouliot.l
silent prayer for the success of our own and allied forces and for the early liberation of the peoples of Europe."
The house will be interested in the order of the day which was given to the troops by General Eisenhower. It is as follows:
" Soldiers, sailors and airmen of the allied expeditionary force: You are about to embark upon the great crusade toward which we have striven these many months. The eyes of the world are upon you. The hopes and prayers of liberty-loving peoples everywhere march with you.
" You will bring about the destruction of the German war machine, the elimination of nazi tyranny over the oppressed peoples of Europe and security for ourselves in a free world.
"Your task will not be an easy one. Your enemy is well trained, well equipped and battle hardened. He will fight savagely.
" But this is the year 1944. Much has happened since the Nazi triumphs of 1940-41.
"The united nations have inflicted upon the Germans great defeat in open battle man to man. Our air offensive has seriously reduced their strength in the air and their capacity to wage war on the ground.
"Our home fronts have given us an overwhelming superiority in weapons and munitions of war and placed at our disposal great reserves of trained fighting men.
"The tide has turned.
"The free men of the world are marching together to victory. I have full confidence in your courage, devotion to duty, and skill in battle.
"We will accept nothing less than full victory.
"Good luck, and let us all beseech the blessing of Almighty God upon this great and noble undertaking."
Hon. members will realize that at this stage it is very difficult indeed to give the house much information of an official and authentic character. It would be a mistake, I think, for me to attempt to give anything in the nature of details relating to the events that have happened within the past twenty-four hours. Fortunately, however, the Prime Minister of Great Britain addressed the House of Commons of the United Kingdom this morning and in the course of his remarks was able to give to the house information which will be of equal interest to all of us. I therefore propose now to give to the house a part of the statement which Mr. Churchill made this morning. I should say that the Prime Minis-

Invasion of Western En: oye
ter preceded his remarks by making a reference" to the significance of the fall of Rome. He dwelt at some length upon what that great event signified in relation to the other events which are taking place at this moment. He then continued as follows:
"I have also to announce to the house that during the night and early hours of this morning, the first of a series of landings in force upon the European continent has taken place.
"In this case, the liberating assault fell upon the coast of France.
"An immense armada of upwards of 4,000 ships, together with several thousand smaller craft, crossed the channel. Mass airborne landings have been successfully effected behind the enemy's lines.
"Landings on the beaches are proceeding at various points at the present time. The fire of shore batteries has been largely quelled. Obstacles which were encountered in the sea have not proved as difficult as was apprehended.
"The Anglo-American allies are sustained by about eleven thousand first line aircraft, which can be drawn upon as may be needed for the purposes of battle.
"I cannot, of course, commit myself to any particular details, as reports are coming in in rapid succession. So far the commanders who are engaged report that everything is proceeding according to plan. And what a plan!
"This vast plan is undoubtedly the most complicated and difficult that has ever occurred. It involves the tides, wind, waves and visibility both from the air and sea standpoints, and the combined employment of land, air and sea forces in the highest degree of intimacy.
"There are already hopes that actual tactical surprise has been attained, and we hope to furnish the enemy with a succession of surprises during the course of the fighting.
"The battle which has now begun will grow constantly in scale and in intensity for many weeks to come, and I shall not attempt to speculate on its course, but this I may say-that complete unity prevails.
"Throughout the allied armies there is a brotherhood in arms between us and our friends in other states. There is complete confidence in the supreme commander, General Eisenhower, and in his lieutenants, and also in the commander of the expeditionary force, General Montgomery.
"The ardour and spirit of the troops, as I saw for myself when they were embarking in the last few days, were splendid to witness. Nothing in the way of equipment, science or forethought has been neglected."
As we await the news of battle there are certain things w'hich I think it would be well for members of this house as well as for the people of Canada to keep in mind. The fact that an allied landing on the continent has taken place is of itself a great feat. It means that after many months of the most careful and detailed planning the enemy has been pushed back at one part of the rim of his fortress. Even so, the task of having landed is but a prelude to the more urgent task of maintaining this first foothold, and of maintaining it so strongly that the enemy cannot dislodge the allied forces. We must expect that initial counter attacks on a small scale will be followed by massed, all-out counter attacks by the mobile and reserve forces of the enemy. These counter attacks may extend over a long period, and it is important that we should not magnify successes which may be achieved.
On a previous occasion, referring to the invasion of Europe, I said:
"This greatest of all tasks must be approached with the utmost foresight,. . . .it will require the most complete preparation. It is the duty of all concerned to see that sound judgment is not impaired by impatience, that nothing that can possibly be foreseen is left to chance. Invasion when it comes must be fortified with as full knowledge, as it is possible to obtain in advance, of every factor that will count for life or death in the balances that to-day are deciding the fate of the world."
The allied offensive launched to-day, as Mr. Churchill has said, is the most complete coordination and integration of effort among all the allied forces.
We must also remember that the enemy has been established for more than four years in the territory which he must now defend. The defensive preparations he has made must be expected to be all that his experience and ingenuity can devise. The enemy strength, while not precisely known, is very formidable.
We must also keep constantly in mind that the supply problem is one of the greatest magnitude because of the fact that most of the implements of war, munitions, food and supplies have to be carried to the front line by sea.
For obvious reasons, it would not be advisable to give information about the strength and disposition of the allied forces or concerning particular formations and commanders taking part in the operations. These will be made known from time to time in official announcements.
Invasion of Western Eurpoe

Conjecture in these anxious days will not do any good, and it may, in fact, give help and comfort to the enemy. This is the more important because of the particular care which has been given to the timing and planning of different operations. It is not to be supposed that the offensive launched to-day will not be followed by other offensives in other parts of Europe both from the sea and over land.
The people of Canada will expect, and it will be the duty of the government to provide, so far as possible, a correct and sober representation of events as they occur. The future, however, must unfold itself.
I am happy to be able to inform the house that official word has already come to the effect that our men have successfully achieved their first objective and are making good progress.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INVASION OF WESTERN EUROPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like on this very compelling occasion to add a word or two to those which have been said by the Prime Minister.
There are no divisions of opinion and no cleavages in thought in this house as we rivet our attention upon the progress of the long-anticipated offensive in Europe. An indescribable sense of oneness pervades this parliament and this nation to-day. The vital and critical character of the present military operations in which our troops are engaged erases all else from the thoughts of the Canadian people. Our armed forces must know that we at home are prepared to reinforce their efforts to the furthest limit. This nation must see to it that whatever is needed to support our fighting forces in men, materials and money is given without stint, without hesitation and without restriction. Nothing less than the best will be good enough for those who give so much for us.
May God be very close to our fighting men and their loved ones at home as this mighty battle for freedom, liberty and democracy proceeds apace.

subtopic: INVASION OF WESTERN EUROPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I assume that all members of the house feel much as I do at the present time, that this is a moment for prayer. All must feel deeply grateful for the protection which the all-Father has given our people; the protection which has enabled us to stand against the apparently invincible forces which confronted us in 1940, and to persevere even until to-day, when it is our privilege to return the attack.
We must feel gratitude also for the miraculous way in which allies have been brought

to our side whose timely assistance rendered it possible for us to survive and whose help, still afforded us, will enable us to prevail against our enemies.
I feel that we all are deeply filled with supplication for the protection of our boys, as far as that may be, and for their success in the arduous task which they now are essaying; and we also, I know, are possessed with the desire to implore the Almighty that we at home may be able to perform our tasks in a way which will make us worthy of the noble boys who represent us overseas.

subtopic: INVASION OF WESTERN EUROPE

It is fitting that a French voice should stress the epoch-making fact that the hour of liberation has now come for France. I am sure of voicing the feelings of all Canadians of French descent in saying that we have been deeply moved by such news. We have not forgotten France, Mr. Speaker, we have not forgotten her, for hundreds and thousands of young French Canadians are perhaps, at this very moment, driving the German invader from the historic shores of old France.
With the permission of this honourable assembly, may I say that the occasion calls for the singing of the national anthem of France.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP EXPEDITING THE 'WORK OP THE SESSION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP EXPEDITING THE 'WORK OP THE SESSION
speechtext:
I should like to take advantage of the feelings which are uppermost in the minds of hon. members at the present moment to make a very earnest plea to the members of the house to join together to seek to expedite as much as we possibly can the further business of this session. I am perfectly sure that with the mind of the country concentrated upon events which will go far to determine the fate of nations for generations to come, individual members in this house,

Business of the House
and the people of Canada generally, will be impatient of utterances made in the House of Commons at this time which are not very much to the point in the discussion of the business which we are here to transact.
I would be the last to wish to impose any restraint upon the utterances of anyone, but I am confident that the feeling throughout Canada is that to-day we have reached one of the most serious moments in the history of the world, and that it is a part of our obligation to human society to avoid irrelevancies as much as possible and to concentrate as completely as we can upon the business before us.
I must say that from looking over the proceedings of the house in the past six weeks it seems to me that we shall not be able, unless we move at a more rapid pace than has been followed thus far, to complete in the course of this year the business that is already indicated on the order paper. I know hon. members do not wish to have the proceedings unduly prolonged. The only way in which the house can control the situation is by each member feeling an individual obligation to do his utmost to further the common will.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP EXPEDITING THE 'WORK OP THE SESSION
speechtext:
What the Prime Minister has said will, I believe, find a very responsive echo in the house generally at this time. I am quite sure it will also be appreciated outside the house as well.	'
I would like to suggest to the Prime Minister one thing-a suggestion that was made before. Perhaps I can make that suggestion now in a way that will be of considerable help to the government and to parliament and will tend to expedite the business of the house. As the Prime Minister knows, we have not been sitting on Wednesdays during this session. I quite appreciate the position in which the government find themselves, and I have no desire to make it more difficult for them. Indeed, as the weeks have passed, I haye had a greater appreciation than ever before of the burdens on the government, but I am going to suggest to the Prime Minister that we sit on Wednesday afternoons and evenings. I suggest that we have none of the preliminary proceedings on Wednesdays which would necessitate the presence here of the ministry, the Prime Minister or the war committee of the cabinet. I suggest that on Tuesday night we adjourn to go on at three o'clock on Wednesday exactly where we left off the night before, without any of the intermediate proceedings, and that we continue until eleven o'clock, with the supper adjournment on Wednesday.
Perhaps that would meet a situation which the Prime Minister finds exceedingly difficult.
Both he and the government want to have some time in which to handle the heavy burdens in the war cabinet, and I offer that suggestion in what I hope is a constructive way, in order that we may be able to utilize not only the cooperation which I am sure the house will give, but also every minute of the time, because everyone in this house wants to have the business disposed of as quickly as possible. If the Prime Minister, myself and others give the lead we shall probably find a responsive following all over the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP EXPEDITING THE 'WORK OP THE SESSION
speechtext: I shall be glad to consider carefully what my hon. friend has said, but I would say that the events of the last twenty-four hours have placed an additional burden on the ministry, much greater than any we have borne heretofore. Whether members of the government are in the house or not, the ministry has to bear the responsibility for what takes place. I would wish to think over very carefully what my hon. friend has suggested. To-morrow it -would not be possible for the house to meet, in the light of what has happened to-day. Whether it will be possible in subsequent weeks, I shall have to consider very carefully with my colleagues. I suggest to my hon. friend, however, that to-morrow and possibly other Wednesdays until we feel we can sit on Wednesdays as well as other days without incurring serious risks, the day might in part be occupied by the whips of the different parties meeting together to see whether they could not come to some arrangement among themselves as to the amount of time it will be necessary to give to different measures, and reach an understanding with regard to methods of expediting the work of the session. That, I understand, is one of the methods employed in the British house. A certain length of time is assigned to particular debates; it is left to the different parties to decide which of their members will speak, and the discussion is limited to the time agreed upon. Something of that sort, I think, will be necessary if we are to get 'through in any reasonable time.

subtopic: MESSAGE OF THANKS FROM PRIME MINISTER PAPANDREOU FOR SHIPMENTS OF FOOD

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MESSAGE OF THANKS FROM PRIME MINISTER PAPANDREOU FOR SHIPMENTS OF FOOD
speechtext:
I received last night the following telegram from the new Prime Minister of Greece in reference to shipments of food which have gone from Canada to Greece. The house will be much interested in its contents. The telegram is as follows:
Cairo, June 5, 1944. The Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
In assuming the premiership of the Royal Hellenic government of national union I wish to express to you and to the government and people of Canada the profound gratitude of the Greek nation for the vital help which they are receiving from your generous country in their appalling plight. Having lived in Greece until a few weeks ago and having shared in the unprecedented burden of famine and oppression which has not succeeded in crushing the spirit of my countrymen I feel entitled to convey to you this recognition of Canada's assistance and also to appeal for the greater possible development of these shipments to Greece without which the Greek nation cruelly decimated as it is would be threatened with total extinction. Please let all Canadians know that the food grown in the rich and free lands of their fine country is helping to save the life of a nation bn whose soil liberty was first born and was constantly defended throughout long centuries, a nation which is now tortured and mutilated

more than ever because it has refused to deny its ancient creed in the freedom and dignity of man.
Papandreou,
Prime Minister of Greece.
To that communication I sent the following reply this morning:
Ottau'a, June 6, 1944. His Excellency George Papandreou,
Prime Minister of Greece,
Cairo, Egypt.
I am deeply grateful to you for your moving message expressing the gratitude of the Greek nation for the shipments of food from Canada. It has been a source of pride and thankfulness to the government and people of Canada that during the past two years they have been able to provide some relief in this manner .to the people of Greece. It is fitting that the ancient seat of human freedom should be sustained during the time of its darkest tribulation by the young and free Canadian people. I trust that the aid already brought to Greece in its struggle for survival will increase in volume until liberation has been achieved. May the day of liberation be near.
W. L. Mackenzie King

Has the Minister of Mines and Resources been requested to meet Indian delegates in con-

Indian Affairs
vention here or to provide room for their accommodation; if so, what provision has been -made?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: MEETING OF INDIAN DELEGATES IN CONVENTION IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to send me an intimation before three o'clock that he proposed to ask this question; and since the matter to which it relates has been the subject of reports in the newspapers and I believe was also mentioned on the radio last evening, perhaps I should answer his question a little more fully than by a mere "yes" or "no".
On May 19 I received a letter from one who purported to be the leader of the Indians of Canada. His name is Jules Sioui, of Loretteville, Quebec. Perhaps I should read the letter. It is as followp:
Dear Sir,
It is my duty to acquaint you with'the final decision of the Indian chiefs of each tribe throughout the country, namely, that without exception they will all be present at the great convention which will be held in Ottawa from the fifth to the tenth of June.
It is understood that you are the general superintendent of Indian affairs but it is known that you have a great number of assistants and agents who are guilty of serious irregularities since many years toward the Indians.
Here is the claim of the Indian people for the next convention which will be held, from the fifth of June; according to them the promises which were made by Her Majesty and others, either by proclamation or treaty, have not been respected either by your department or by the government itself. Therefore, the Indian people want it to be known that it cannot live and is not willing to go on living as it does, in a state which is not tolerable. That is why they will have a meeting with the object of dictating the future of the nation for their offspring.
Being the leader of the Indian people I am requested to hereby notify you that the Indian chiefs ask that a convenient place be prepared for the holding of their meeting -which will last five days at least; and in view of the scarcity of rooms in the hotels, we also ask you to take the necessary steps for the erection of large tents where they will be able to sleep. It is understood that they will pay the installation cost of those tents.
I think it is necessary to draw your attention to the fact that the Indian chiefs are determined to be peaceful and gentle, but they have decided that your department and the government will have to change the situation from A to Z, believe it or not.
Yours truly,
Jules Sioui,
Leader of the Indians of Canada
Post Office, Loretteville, Que. *
My reply to that was as follows:
M. E. J. Bastien,
Indian Agent,
Village Des Hurons, Quebec.
Please advise Jules Sioui that his letter of May 15 has received my personal attention and that the department does not recognize his leadership of any group of Indians in Canada
100-225J
and also that it is my earnest desire that the proposed convention should not be proceeded with as there is no accommodation here. Extreme pressure of business makes it impossible for the authorities to meet a large gathering. Director of Indian Affairs will be ready to receive a small delegation of about six Indians if recommended by their agents.
T. A. Crerar.
In spite of this, Jules Sioui turned up yesterday with a number of Indians. There may be some chiefs in this group of Indians whose presence in Ottawa has received considerable publicity, but I doubt if there are many. Sioui has no standing whatever as leader of the Indians in Canada. Yesterday he sent a request that I meet him and the delegation. I refused to do so, for two reasons. In the first place he is not the leader of the Indians of Canada; in the second place Sioui has been convicted of offences twice in the last six or seven years and has served gaol sentences. Not only that, but at the present time he is before the courts on a charge which, if ultimately proven, will land him in gaol again. I am doing no injustice to the Indians of Canada when I refuse to see him. I have sent word to the Indians present here in Ottawa that if they wish to appoint a small delegation of five or six I shall be glad to see them in my office in the House of Commons at five-thirty this afternoon, but I would not receive Sioui if he came with them as a delegate. I think that answers the question of my hon. friend.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
I should like to ask the Minister of Transport if an inquiry will be held by the wreck commissioner
Motor Launch "Olga'
COMiMONS
into the wreck of a motor excursion launch called the Olga on Sunday last, at Port Stanley on lake Erie, in which some fifteen passengers were drowned. The act requires an immediate investigation. I should like to know also what life-saving equipment is carried by boats of this kind, what aids to navigation are provided, and what precautions are taken.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Transport) :
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO ACCIDENT RESULTING IN LOSS OF LIFE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Broadview was kind enough to give me notice of the question he has just asked. In reply I may say that on Sunday, June 4, a motor cruiser named Olga capsized at Port Stanley, Ontario, with the result that the lives of several persons were lost. On Monday morning arrangements were made to hold a preliminary inquiry under section 548 of the Canada Shipping Act, 1934. Captain Fred S. Slocombe, supervising examiner of masters and mates, Toronto, was instructed by telephone to hold an immediate inquiry. He left Toronto yesterday morning, accompanied by the chairman of the board of steamship inspection. It is expected that a complete report of the preliminary inquiry will be available in two or three days.
Replying to the second part of the question, the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, provides for the making of regulations for the safety and protection of people using small craft as well as large boats. Regulations were made and published; the last issue of the publication was 1937, and it was entitled, "Regulations respecting life-saving appliances." One of the regulations provides that the owners of small boats of more than five tons capacity shall protect the lives of those using such boats by providing life buoys, and further that every ship to which the regulations apply shall carry an appropriate number of life jackets, not less than the number of persons which the ship is certified to carry. Further, motor boats in excess of five tons gross tonnage carrying passengers are required to be inspected by a steamship inspector, and to have a certificate of inspection given by him. From time to time notice of these regulations is given to the public; the last notice was published on June 1, 1943, and must have been posted at or near Port Stanley, as directions were given that such notices should be posted in all our ports, calling the attention of motor boat owners to the provisions of the regulations and the shipping act with regard to equipment for the protection of people using such boats.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REPORTED CESSATION OF RATIONING IN THE UNITED STATES-CANADIAN POLICY
speechtext:
Yesterday at page 3519 of Hansard the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) asked this question:
In view of the fact that the United States do not now ration sugar, will the minister make a statement as to the present position in Canada, and indicate whether the restrictions in this country will likewise be lifted?
I have made inquiries, and find that the United States is still rationing sugar on substantially the same basis as it is rationed in Canada. The sugar administrator informs me that he thinks there is no chance of the United States abandoning the rationing of sugar, and certainly no consideration is being given to the lifting of the restrictions here.

speechtext:

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should like to ask some questions in connection with this item for expenditures for the purpose of looking after the interests of Canadian nationals abroad. Last night the minister said that this expenditure referred to Canadian nationals in enemy countries who could not get home, and that the money would be spent for clothing, food, and purposes of that kind.
I would remind the minister that we are altogether relying on the International Red Cross, with its headquarters at Geneva, Switzerland. Switzerland is a neutral country, and it is the allies' protecting power. It acts as a sort of caretaker, and as a protecting power for the allies. The International Red Cross is located in that country; it communicates with and inspects camps, and looks after parcels sent to enemy countries. I fail to see why we should depend only upon one protecting power for the carrying out of this work, because in my view it is the first duty of the government to look after these nationals and prisoners of war. The same observations would apply to prisoners of war-although I realize they are not included in this item. There should be some inspection as well as that of the protecting power; we ought not to have to rely solely on Switzerland. For instance, we have Russia as an ally. Some of our nationals are in Japan, and yet we depend upon the protecting power, Switzerland, for the protection of those nationals. One of our allies, Russia, might be able to help in respect of our nationals and prisoners in Japan. The same applies to Germany, and to all other enemy countries.
We should be more active, not only in connection with Canadian nationals in those enemy countries, but also in respect of prisoners of war. In my view the government itself should take some action in these matters, direct or indirect, and not depend entirely on the International Red Cross. Sometimes they cannot do all that should be done-although we realize they have done [DOT]magnificent work. These nationals and prisoners of war should not have to depend entirely upon a protecting power which in turn depends upon the International Red Cross. Surely the government could be a little more active.
The minister gave a long list of neutral countries, but there was one he did not mention, namely, southern Ireland. She is a neutral country, and some of our Canadian pilots are there. They have landed there and cannot get out. I have been told that they are not looked after, through this vote. The first duty of the government is to follow this through as far as possible and not rely
entirely upon one protecting power. Let us get better reports than we are getting from Switzerland. While we have a diplomatic arrangement with that country to look after prisoners of war and nationals in enemy countries, something more active than that is necessary so that we may know what is going on over there. For instance, the other day some of those nationals might have been shot, the way some of the prisoners of war were. In those circumstances we would not have known where we stood.
On this seventy-second day of the session we should have more information in the house with respect to Canadian nationals and prisoners of war than we have at the present time. I should like to have a reply from the minister, because complaints have been made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Last night I explained the purpose of the vote. This is not drawn upon to look after prisoners of war. The Red Cross have that work exceptionally well organized, from all the information made available to the public. They made several appeals to Canada, with very generous response. This item is to be administered by the director of the immigration branch, through the agency of the protecting power, to assist Canadian nationals, some of whom may be interned and others of whom may not be interned, but who might be in want because of the circumstances in which, through no fault of their own, they find themselves.
The important question whether or not the government is doing enough to care for prisoners of war is one which does not come under this vote. That is a question which might be taken up on some other occasion. As I understand it, under international conventions the German authorities are expected to provide for allied prisoners of war who may be in Germany the same accommodation and food they supply to their own troops. I believe I am correct in that. On the other hand, that is the standard in Canada so far as German prisoners of war are concerned. The chief question raised by the hon. member, however, cannot be covered by this vote.

Item agreed to.
To provide single minimum cost of transportation of wives and dependents of members of the Canadian forces overseas, $100,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is the minister able to state the number of soldiers' wives coming from England and the number of children accompanying them? Is it, necessary to assist all of them, or do some of them pay their own way?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The government pays the passage of these dependents to Canada. From the beginning of the war to the present time approximately fifteen hundred have been brought to Canada. In the fiscal year 1942-43 257 were brought back at an expenditure of $22,651. The number of warrants for transportation issued to dependents for the period April 1, 1943, to January 4, 1944, was 580, and the expenditure for the last fiscal year up to February 29 was $23,299.51. But the number of these people coming back week by week and month by month is increasing, and consequently we are asking for this larger sum. I cannot tell the committee whether all of it will be required; I cannot tell them whether it will be sufficient. As regards many of these war appropriation estimates all we can make is an approximation, and we hope we are fairly near the mark in the amount we are asking for here.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Some time ago I saw a newspaper item to the effect that 11,000 of our soldiers had married overseas. In due course their wives will have to be brought to Canada. In the meantime they will have some children, and the aggregate number requiring transportation will be quite large. I have been wondering whether the minister has asked for a large enough vote.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I believe the number of Canadians who have married overseas is substantially larger than the figure mentioned by my hon. friend, and it may be, if the war ends soon and a movement to Canada upon a considerable scale is begun, this amount will be insufficient; if it is, probably we can get a further amount out of the war appropriation vote. But it is not likely that there will be a very large movement of dependents during the present fiscal year. In the first place, where a soldier has married overseas and has one or two children, his family will remain there until he returns; indeed the likelihood

is that he will return before his family. That is a problem which has to be worked out. Then there is the question of transportation facilities.

speechtext: Over here?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Across from the other side to Canada. When the war is over several million troops will have to be brought back to North America. The officers think that this amount is sufficient to meet the needs of the current year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does the vote cover the return of soldiers' wives who went to Great Britain with their husbands?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There might have been a few in the air service who went over very early, immediately after the outbreak of the war, but later the movement of women and children was stopped. Therefore, soldiers' wives and families were not allowed to leave Canada and go to Britain. A very serious problem arose at the end of the last war. During the course of that war thousands of dependents of Canadian soldiers, wives and children, went to Britain and had to be brought back. There were over 50,000 at the end of the war. There are two or three reasons why we did not want a repetition of that after this war. There was a greater danger in this war than there was at the time of the last war in having the dependents over there, and furthermore Britain was hard pressed for food and it did not make sense to allow the dependents of Canadian soldiers to go to Britain and thus add to the difficulties there. The movement was therefore stopped. The movement which this vote will cover will be in all instances that of dependents of members of the armed forces who went overseas.

speechtext: Does the request for the return of the wife come from the soldier or from the wife?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: What is the general policy in connection with the return of these people? Some men may have been killed and some may be fighting in the army overseas. Does the request come from the soldier himself or from his wife?

These have to do, mainly though not altogether, with cases where the soldier has been wounded and is invalided home. He may be discharged for one reason or another and comes back to Canada, and under those circumstances, if he has married since he went to Britain, he
wishes to have his family back, and we want to bring them back. The vote is for that purpose.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is the consent of the soldier always obtained before the request is granted?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am thinking more particularly of soldiers still over there, soldiers still in action, and I was wondering whether the request came from the wife or the soldier. The consent of the soldier would have to be obtained, would it not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

I do not think his wife would want to run away from him over there, nor do I think he would want to run away from his recently acquired wife. These things are worked out by mutual arrangement. I do not know of any cases of the kind suggested by my hon. friend.

speechtext: There are over 1,300 of the children still in Canada. speechtext:
I want to congratulate the Minister of Mines and Resources upon the interest he has taken in the welfare of these children. This afternoon the Prime Minister read a cable from the Premier of Greece, sent from Cairo, to the effect that the help sent by Canada had been received by the Greeks. That help was badly needed, and the cable indicated, that what had been sent by Canada had reached its destination. If I understood correctly what was said by the minister this item of $75,000 is in connection with children already in Canada. I suggest to the minister that something should be done for the children of Europe. It could be done through the Red Cross, in the same way that parcels are' sent to allied prisoners of war in concentration camps in Germany or the occupied countries. The distress of these children is incredible. I have here a book by Miss Therese Bonney, a lady who is very much interested in welfare work; this book is illustrated, and I will send it to the minister. The preface is in these words:
This is the tale, not of one, but of too many European countries, the story of an eye witness . . . visual testimony . . . not words . . . not propaganda .	.	. reality. There are no
staged pictures ... no misleading captions.
With my camera I have made this record in France, Spain, England, Sweden and Finland.

This is incidental. They might have been taken m a score of other countries to-day. I have written this story with my lens. This is the truth for which I vouch.
The captions under the pictures go on in this way:
It was not so long ago-the children of Europe trooped to class. They went to school-learned their three R's; led happy normal lives at home-at play. Then-war was declared. They too read the news. Suddenly-their little voices were silenced-communications were severed and then-we knew no more. Children played while men dug trenches. Then-they too prepared for war. When the day came there was only an hour-to leave. They took to the road. Tiny tots-packs on their backs. Heavy burdens for weary mothers. From time to time they rested; the old-the young; slept anywhere, everywhere; took refuge in barns. Like grownups they too were wounded. They tried so hard to save what they loved if only-a doll. Planes overhead. They understood so little-between air raids; a moment's respite. So exhausted. At times it seemed almost impossible to trudge on. To concentration camps they went, the children, all over Europe. Mothers cradled them while fathers died at their side of neglect and tuberculosis. There the Quakers gave them paper and pencil and they tried to learn. They took it all so seriously, opened their eyes so wide; faced it so courageously-so gallantly. Timidly-they climb to would-be homes in gutted houses. In wind and rain they beg- they search for food; and so often all they find is rotten oranges. Shoeless, hungry, they stay in bed. One shoeless-rags. They go from door to door; sleep-in mangers. Victims-of a civil war, a defeat, an invasion; they face a strange life. Larders empty; "no bread-useless to insist" chalked on bakery doors. "Plus de pain; inutile d'insister." No food at home; long lines in school; one meal a day. They fold their hands in prayer and thank God for that little. Trust the world so implicitly. So few have understood; the Quakers, Red Crosses -nuns. That bread becomes not only the staff of life but the staff of resistance and oppression. They-not the Germans-get the little sent and they try so hard to say thank you.
I want to show this to the minister. I wonder if he cannot do anything for these little children who are dying of hunger in occupied Europe. Those who are here are well fed and well looked after, but these are the young men of the future generation. I hope they will never be exposed to the horrors of war. This is a tragic matter. The situation is so bad in France that little children cannot go to school unless they have a certificate from the doctor to the effect that they do not suffer from tuberculosis. Children are dying in countless numbers in Europe at the present time, and now is the time to do something for them. A society was organized in Montreal for the purpose of helping these children.
I have a friend in Westmount, an eminent artist, Mr. J. R. Spendlove, who has taken a special interest in this matter. He has done as much for these little children as Miss Therese Bonney has done in Europe. He 
wonders, for instance, why the work of the Save the Children Society of Montreal was halted. People were ready to do something. I received a letter from one of my confreres in Beauce county, who told me he wanted to do something, but all their hopes were in vain; nothing could be done. This afternoon, when we came back to the chamber after having listened to His Majesty the King, I went to see the Prime Minister and showed him some of these pathetic pictures. I do not know if that society in Montreal had the approval of the Minister of National War Services, but where is that minister to-day? He is supposed to look after all charitable organizations. This is a matter that should have come under the Minister of Mines and Resources, with his big heart, but now is the time to see that something is done, something more than words, something concrete. Our granaries are full of wheat, some of which we have sent to Greece. There is no reason why something should not be sent to the other countries of Europe. I ask the Minister of Mines and Resources and his colleagues who are listening to me now to urge this matter upon the Prime Minister, who is surely well disposed, so that something may be done at the earliest possible opportunity. Now that the invasion has commenced it will be possible to reach some of these people directly, but in the case of those who cannot be reached directly some help may be given through the Red Cross. I urge this upon the minister, and I hope that something may be done.

Following the very ,moving appeal by the hon. member for Temiscouata I want to say that I think he has done a distinct service in bringing this matter to the attention of the committee. This book of pictures which he has sent to my desk reveals a shocking condition of affairs in the districts in which these photographs were taken. Unquestionably we have no conception in Canada of the terrible plight of hundreds of thousands-yes, millions of men and women, and particularly children in, Europe to-day. To bring a measure of relief to these unfortunate people is one of the purposes of the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, commonly called UNRRA, which was set up several months ago, and upon which Canada is prominently represented. Under UNRRA the people of Canada are pledged to provide a certain quota of relief. By far the greater portion is to come from the United States, and Great Britain andi other countries are also pledged to assist. I have no doubt whatsoever that effective steps are now being taken to organize relief for those poor people, and if the steps already taken

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
prove insufficient, there would be no people or government in the world with any of the decent instincts of humanity that would refuse further assistance.
In the moving speech he delivered this afternoon the hon. member for Temiseouata has brought to the attention of the committee a matter to which we should give full consideration.

It would seem that the war estimates of the Department of Mines and Resources are almost through. Therefore at this time may I pay a tribute to those of our war guests who came from Great Britain to Canada. Before doing so, however, may I add what I believe is a well-deserved tribute to the sympathetic and moving appeal made this afternoon by the hon. member for Temiseouata. It shows that in the House of Commons members have big hearts, and that they are prepared to take their stand for the rights of humanity in which this nation is so deeply interested.
Many of our war guests are now returning to their homes, some to serve in the armed forces and some for other causes, and for that reason I believe that as a parliament we might properly express our deep appreciation of having had them with us. They have been an inspiration to the whole country, particularly to the people in those communities in which they have been located. Among the guests who came to Canada were some seventy or eighty little girls from St. Hilda's college at Whitby, England. They were taken to one of the larger homes in Erindale, in my constituency, where arrangements had been made for them. I have been to that home on occasion, and the impression the little girls made upon those of us who from time to time went to see them, and to see the work being done for them by the sisters, is one which will remain with us for a long time.
I believe that the war guests have done something for the Canadian people, and I hope on the other hand that we have done something for them. I believe that their presence here has brought the people of the United Kingdom and those of Canada just a little bit closer because, in the final analysis, there is nothing like children to bring about that result.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

The observation of the hon. member for New Westminster prompts me to join in the hope that they will come back. I believe that we may expect something of that kind, because I have no doubt the hospitality and welcome extended to them has been deeply appreciated.
The hon. member's remark prompts me to add something further. In the last three or four months I have had particularly heavy overseas correspondence from men who lived in my constituency but who are now overseas. Now, more than ever before, they are writing home and saying that they have friends from one or other parts of the empire, or from Great Britain itself, who are anxious to learn if this would not be a good place to come when the war is over. They want to know what the possibilities are. They want to know what jobs there will be. If I have answered one, I am sure I have answered scores of letters in the last two or three months giving *information along those lines. This is information sought by friends of our boys overseas. They have liked those boys, and because of that they think they would like our country.
I have thought it well at this time to take a moment or two of the committee's time to add this word of appreciation in respect of one of those little things brought about by the war, one of those things which, as time goes by, may develop into a very big thing

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members may recall I mentioned a few days ago that, when taking up civil estimates, I would make a general statement on external affairs, and would be prepared to discuss individual items in the committee at whatever length hon. members might desire. My hope is that it will not be necessary to discuss on these war appropriation estimates, in any detail in any event, the matters that would be discussed on the civil estimates.
I might explain that when the war came on, the Department of External Affairs necessarily assumed a number of additional duties and began to perform services which had not been performed in peace time. It is apparent now that many of these services will for the most part have to be continued after the war is over. I might illustrate; for example, a number of new legations and embassies have been opened during the war. In making appropriation for these services where they have arisen ,n time of war we have voted some of the moneys required under the war appropriation. This year, in order to make matters a little clearer, we have included many of these services in the civil estimates account rather than in the war appropriation estimates. Hon. members will see we are asking for smaller amounts in the war appropriation estimates than we did a year ago.. That does not mean that there will be less expenditure on these services. It means that we have transferred to the civil estimates expenditures we were formerly voting under the war appropriation. All the three items here set forth, departmental administration and passport office, representation abroad, and sundry services could be discussed under the civil estimates as they will come up then, and I would hope that they might be discussed then rather than now.
Mr. KNOWLES; In idew of what the Prime Minister has just said about transferring the expenditures to civil estimates, may I ask why he does not transfer all of them? Are the amounts that are still here in the nature of war estimates?

Provision for such may appear under the war appropriation estimates. If they continue after the war they will thereafter appear in the civil estimates.

speechtext:
Two
instances were brought to my attention of bulletins sent out by the wartime information board covering national selective service. I took occasion to write, protesting against the duplication, to the gentleman whom I see in front of me. I must say that he answered very courteously but without very much conviction, to me at all events. There is duplication and some of the information given out is not even supplementary. I am sorry I have not my file with me. I could show the Prime Minister exactly what I mean if I had it here. Two of the bulletins I refer to were just pure duplication. If the board have to be busy-and I suppose they have to or they could not justify themselves- care should be taken to see that there is no overlapping, because all this comes out of the taxpayers' money. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Last year the appropriation and work of the wartime information board were very fully explained and discussed, and I do not feel that hon. members would wish me at this time to make any extended remarks.
The work of the boardJ has been carried on and has been expanded considerably during the past year to fill strong and obvious needs for its services. Plans for this fiscal year are for the continuation of activities on about the present level. The amount of the board's estimates is small in relation to the need for the spreading of knowledge about wartime Canada both abroad and inside the country itself.
The events of to-day bring home the desire of all Canadians to have all possible information about their country and its place in the world and the glorious record our forces are making abroad. Information leads to understanding and understanding to common action.
Information has played an important part and has still a great role to play in the winning of the war and the laying of a solid foundation for peace. It was in pursuance of these objects that the board was set up to meet a real need.
The remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury were directed toward a publication known as "Labour Facts," issued by the wartime information board to editors of labour journals to industrial establishments and trades unions. The bulletin was issued after a very careful survey had been made which indicated that there was a strong need for such a publication. I have a copy under my hand.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Why does the parliamentary assistant say that? I will tell him that the publication came to me from a big industrialist who said that he had already received the information many times from the Department of Labour and that there was nothing new in this publication.
As to the necessity for this board generally, my understanding of the setting-up of this board vras that it was to diffuse proper information in the United States, where there was a misunderstanding as to Canada's war effort. I applauded that because I thought they were in need of information over there as to Canada's aims and objectives; as to what we did, how we did it and why we did it. But the work of this board is expanding at an alarming rate. More than that, it ignores the public press of this country. Most of the stuff this board sends out, the newspaper men tell me, finds its way into the wastepaper basket.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
This sheet, "Labour
Facts", was sent out, as I say, to meet a need which was strongly expressed. That material was not made available in any other form. This is not of the nature of news; it is information bearing on labour questions; and I can read to the committee, if it wishes me to take the time, some part of this file of commendations received from representatives of trades unions and industrial establishments and industrial organizations, commending this publication and stating that it meets a long-felt need. May I read one, from Mr. A. R. Mosher, president of the Canadian Congress of Labour:
For several months the wartime information board has been publishing a bulletin entitled "Labour Facts" for the use of labour publications in Canada. I believe that that bulletin should be read by labour editors on publication and that the material in it, both text and illustrations, should be utilized to the fullest extent. It is almost impossible to keep up with activities in the field of labour on a national and international scale, and much interesting material that would be overlooked ordinarily is brought together in "Labour Facts" in such a way that it can be reprinted directly or

War Appropriation-External Affairs
rewritten to meet the requirements of the editor. May I commend "Labour Facts" to all labour editors and urge that they cooperate with the wartime information board by giving wider circulation to the material it contains.
There is a very large file of similar correspondence. This publication does not take the place of regular news services; it does provide material which editors concerned in dealing with labour questions can use in such form as they wish, and they do use it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Does the parliamentary assistant suggest that this is any more than a collection board of material which is already sent out by the labour department? That is my understanding of what it is, and whether or not Mr. Mosher has received this material in a convenient form suitable for his purposes, or whether labour editors have received it, I say as a fact that what is sent out and distributed in this pamphlet was already distributed by the Department of Labour, and is a duplication. That is what I am told.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: A reference to the publication itself will indicate that it is not a duplication. On the other hand, it does present in various forms material which has already been sent it by the labour department, but in addition it presents material bearing on the treatment of labour questions in other countries of the British commonwealth including the United Kingdom, and in the United States, and brings to the attention of those dealing with labour matters information of a general nature which is interesting and which has a definite .usefulness in Canada. If you look at volume 1, No. 4, which I have in my hand, you see the headlines in one column, "Labour in Other Lands". "U.S. Trades Unions Increase Membership". Then there is another heading, "Aussies Say Unions 15-7 per cent of Population". "Ford Co. in Britain Signs Union Agreement". And so on. It presents in this particular column information which would not ordinarily be available in any other form. It also collects information which is available in some other form and puts it in the most presentable and most useful form for the purposes of these editors.

speechtext:

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: The hon. member's information is not correct. This is a concise statement of developments in public affairs and in the war effort throughout the dominion. It is sent by air mail to Canadian diplomatic missions, trade commissioners, British embassies and legations, in Central and South America, to the various departments of information, broadcasting and government, to the head offices of a limited number of Canadian exporting firms who have expressed the desire to have it. All these cannot receive the information quickly by any other service. The need was expressed and this publication meets it. It is a single sheet on airmail paper and goes out daily. It is the only way these diplomatic missions and others living abroad receive prompt information about events in Canada. My hon. friend referred to some of the items as if they were mistaken. I have not seen any cases of inaccuracy.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I was told by a member of the war information board that it was sent to newspapers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
It may be sent to newspapers at their own request if they cannot get ordinary news or other services, but it is not sent to newspapers generally.
With regard to " Canadian Churches and the War," this publication is sent out to ministers of non-Roman Catholic churches. It was decided, after conferring with the committee of heads of churches presided over by the primate of the Anglican church, that this would be a useful service. It was to supply a need which the ministers themselves expressed that this service was undertaken. This publication matches a similar service given in the United Kingdom to the churches there. There is a corresponding service that goes to Catholic churches in Canada, and that was agreed to after discussions with the cardinal himself, who expressed his sympathy with the project. In these bulletins material is largely collected from publications in England, in the United States and in other countries as well as in Canada, bearing directly on the work of the churches in connection with the war and the organization of peace after the war.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I have one bulletin which says, "Roosevelt and Wilkie define functions," et cetera. That is January, 1944. Do these go to all the churches or just to the Roman Catholic, the United Church and the Church of England?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The first publication I
mentioned goes to all churches of Protestant denominations, and to all non-Roman Catholic churches. " Nouvelles Catholiques " goes to Roman Catholic churches.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext:

fMr. Claxton.]
My hon. friend mentioned "Canadian Affairs." "Canadian Affairs" was started at the express request of Genera! McNaughton and was referred to in the debate last year. It has been continued, and I have here in a folder expressions of the highest commendation of this publication from officers commanding units from one end of Canada to the other as well as from many units in the United Kingdom. The publication corresponds very closely to a similar one previously issued in Great Britain by the United Kingdom authorities for the service of their troops there.
My hon. friend did not mention "Canada at War", which has the largest circulation of any publication of the wartime information board. That is a publication that is recognized as unique. "Canada at War" is recognized everywhere as the most compact and informative information bulletin issued in any country to-day. Hon. members have all seen the illustrated number which was issued in March and I can assure them that it has received the widest possible praise both inside and outside Canada.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister said that he was not in a position to accept the allegation that inaccuracies appeared in these publications. I would remind him of one. Earlier this session he was putting through a small supplementary vote in connection with refugees, and I called attention to the fact that the February number of "Canada at War" gave a list of dates in the month of January and asserted that a consignment of refugees, I believe 250, had arrived in Canada from the Iberian peninsula that month. Investigation had shown me that it had not yet been decided that they should come, much less had come, and I think the Prime Minister himself had been misled by that information. He will remember that these refugees not only had not come but did not come for some weeks after that.
Another instance of inaccuracy in "Canada at War" was brought before the committee last evening by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi, a particularly displeasing one to the people of British Columbia, where it was asserted that seventy-five per cent of the Japanese in Canada were Canadian born. As the Prime Minister knows, that is a very difficult question in British Columbia, particularly at this time. It is unfortunate that such a misleading statement as that should have come out in "Canada at War". The real figures were placed on Hansard, this session, last session and the session before, and I cannot understand how those who produce "Canada at War" could have made those two mistakes, both of which have come particularly

War Appropriation-External Affairs
to my attention. I do not see how it could happen if they collect the facts, sift and examine them carefully before allowing them to go into print.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The hon. member is quite right in his reference to the statement about the coming of refugees in "Canada at War"; that statement was based on information which had not been properly verified and it was not correct. We are very much indebted to him for pointing it out.
With regard to the percentage of Japanese born in Canada, I have not the figure and I am sure we are very glad indeed to get that correction too. I point out that those publications are issued fairly widespread. "Canada at War" has a large circulation, I think I am right in saying that the hon. member is one of the few people who have ever detected any error of fact in that publication.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I detected one which was admitted, but we did not discuss it publicly. It was a terrible thing to put in this publication.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
When one takes into
account the amount of statistical information it contains and the difficulty of securing adequate secretarial and editorial staff in these days I think it will be seen that the record is a fairly good one, all things considered.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
It seems to be a popular indoor sport to criticize the wartime information board, and since I sit on the opposition side I suppose I might be expected to indulge in that sport; but I am going to vary it a bit and say one or two things on the other side.
I agree in part with the criticism that there is a certain amount of material that is not all it should be, and that there is considerable waste, but in the main I think the job the wartime information board has set itself to, namely, the collecting and disseminating of information on all possible subjects relating to the war-time situation and also the task of getting informative material through to the members of the forces, is one that had to be tackled, and I would hope that from the floor of this house we might not try to discourage the board but that we might offer constructive criticism in order that the work of this board might be improved.
I should like to say a word about two publications. One has already been mentioned, namely, "Canadian Affairs". The other is "Canada Digest". Although I have some criticisms that I might offer about them in a moment, I think they are very good publications, and in this I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver North who made commendable references to them a moment ago. Having said that, may I offer one or two suggestions which I hope will be constructive? I think we have to face this fact, that politics is an important factor in the life of any democratic country; certainly it is in the life of this country. There is no use in tiying to evade that issue; there is no use in trying to be supra-political in talking about our national affairs.
In this country we have several major political parties. They take definite stands. They are all very active, and a great many people feel that the future of this country depends upon which of those parties rise to the top out of the general situation in which we find ourselves. Bearing that in mind, I think the wartime information board, both in the reference papers that it is preparing for use generally at home and in publications that it
3584	COMMONS
War Appropriation-External Affairs
prepares for the forces, should collect and give more information about other political groups, in addition to the party now in power. For example, a commendable series is reaching my desk right now. I do not receive all the material that the hon. member for Peterborough West receives, and on that score I feel a little bit slighted. One commendable series that is coming to me is one in which post-war planning information is being collected-

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I mentioned that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: The hon. member mentioned that, yes. I have read that material closely and I have not yet seen anything in it but the plans of the government now in power. It is a good idea to collect that material and make it available, but I think that not only .would the wartime information board save itself from criticism but it would be doing a job that it ought to do if it also collected the plans of the Progressive Conservative party, assuming they have some clans.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: We lertainly have.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Also plans of tire C.C.F., which we print from time to time and publish in books that members of this house are only too glad to buy.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: After all they cannot transport libraries overseas.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I am quite enjoying the cross-fire that is going on here, but at the same time I am serious and I think hon. members agree with me that if information is to be collected about plans being drafted by responsible bodies in Canada, that material should include not only the material of one party which happens to be the government in power but also the material of the other responsible parties of this country. I feel that the same principle should be given effect to in "Canadian Affairs" and in "Canada Digest". I would therefore suggest that there should be articles in "Canadian Affairs" on the activities of other political groups. The men overseas are interested in what is going on at home. Many of them have been away for quite a few years. They do not know what has developed in the meantime. It seems to me that the wartime information board would be doing its job just that much better if it gave information about other groups. I would suggest that the best place to get authentic information about the Progressive Conservative party is not from us or from the Liberals but from the Progressive

Conservative party. When I say that, my hon. friends to the right do not interrupt me, I notice. The same thing applies to the C.C.F. The best place to get information about our party is not from our enemies-

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The
trouble with my hon. friend is that the members of his party do not all agree. One fellow in British Columbia says one thing, and another fellow here says another.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
-but from us. Similarly with the "Canada Digest". Articles by or about the political leaders of other groups might be reprinted.
As I said a few moments ago, I feel that we have to be realistic about this word "politics". So often it is suggested that there is something underhanded about it, that we should not get "political"; but the plain fact is that politics is an important factor in our Canadian life; it always has been and is definitely so at the present time. I would urge the wartime information board to try to be not just a board of the government but a board of the people of Canada; to aim at collecting and supplying information, both in the reference material provided here at home and the material provided to members of the forces, concerning all the groups and all the activities in Canada at the present time.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I want to register my protest against the underlying theory of the hon. member's proposal. What is it? That in wartime the money of the taxpayers of this country should be utilized in disseminating political propaganda. He objects, and perhaps properly, that the information disseminated by the wartime information board is political propaganda in favour of the government of the day. I think there is a good deal in that charge; I believe it is one of the charges one might justly bring against this board. But let us view the thing from its wider aspect. If the government in charge is entitled to do what it is doing, the hon. member says that we should be allowed [DOT]-meaning his party-to have our views disseminated at public expense in wartime, and the Progressive Conservative party should have the same privilege. Why does he stop there? We have in this house representatives of the bloc populaire; why should they not have their views disseminated at public expense through these government publications? Then we have the Canadian party. It is not large, it is true, but at times it is vocal; and why should he not have his views dis-

War Appropriation-External Affairs
seminated in the same way? I need only go down the whole gamut to reduce this whole thing to an absurdity.
The fact of the matter is that not one dollar of this money should be utilized for political propaganda in behalf of any party, and I know that in principle the Prime Minister will agree with that statement. I believe the *distinction he will make is this. He will say that the plans of the government for the future are not in the nature of political propaganda, that they are statements of government policy. Well, the dividing line there is too narrow for me. I do not think any of this money, ought to be spent in disseminating the views of any particular party with respect to any economic proposals, for the future or otherwise. I do not think the taxpayers of this country will agree to expenditures of that kind; certainly I am not going to agree. No matter what may be the sins of the government in this regard, I am sure they vvould not agree either. What about Tim Buck? Why should he not get his oar in also?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: He has it in now.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: He uses the CBC.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I did not know his propaganda was appearing in "Canada at War" and other government publications. I know he is trying with all his might to attach himself to some party. First he tried the socialist party, but they repudiated him. Now he is knocking gently at the door of the Prime Minister, and as far as I am concerned the right hon. gentleman is welcome to him. I notice that the only political parties he has not sought to associate with are the Social Crediters and the very respectable Progressive Conservative party, to which I belong, and I tell him now that if he knocks at our door he knocks in vain.
But let us be serious about this matter for a moment. I ask the Prime Minister to see to it and give instructions that any information disseminated by these boards shall be objective and shall not be open to the criticism that it is political propaganda. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made the definite charge that material which has gone out is propaganda on behalf of the government. I believe a great many people will agree with that view. It may be arguable, but I do not think much issue can be taken with that statement if you consider as a whole what has been sent out. Certainly I would object to any of my taxes-and I pay a good deal-being used to disseminate my political views. I shall do that in some other
way. I would register the strongest possible protest I could summon to my aid against sending out propaganda in favour of the socialistic policies of my hon. friends to the left. I am not going to help pay for that if I can help it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
May I just reply to my hon. friend and say that I would very strongly resent government publications being used for purposes of political propaganda. I think all the boards understand that, and I am perfectly sure the members of this board seek in their publications to avoid what may be regarded as propaganda and to give only facts.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I
should like to ask the parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister what Canada pays towards the united nations information office at CIO Fifth avenue, New York?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
