speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: It is a contribution to the work of the office. The united nations information office is one of the instruments of the united nations. Quite a number of those nations contribute to the work of the office. The costs are allocated among them, and Canada's contribution between those dates was the amount I have mentioned.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I should like to call the attention of the committee to some matters in connection .with this wartime information board which I think are of most importance, particularly in view of the changed position in the war. As hon. members know, the appointment of this particular information board was, in my opinion, a reflection upon the press of this country. It showed not only a lack of appreciation, but a lack of confidence in the press of the country, which had done such splendid work during the last war, in the present war, and in the long years of depression between.
I am very much surprised, in view of the changed conditions in the war, that the government is now anxious to continue this policy of spending nearly a million dollars in the United States to educate the people over there.

War Appropriation-External Affairs
I have looked into this situation very carefully. There was a debate on July 13 last year with respect to this same subject matter. It was pointed out at that time that some of the leading people wanted us to open offices in New York, Chicago, San Francisco, and many other places in the United States. What for? To try to educate the people of the United States about Canada, and all that kind of thing. As a result of this the parliamentary assistant, and others, invited many members of the press to come to Canada. Fifteen or twenty of them looked over the country. They came, they saw, but they did not conquer. They went back home and wrote a few articles in their newspapers-and in some cases Canada paid in gold of the realm for it, paid for ads in those little papers- pages of ads in papers. They went into the county papers, and all that kind of thing.
The government forgets to realize that we have to-day a regular expeditionary force. Where? In the United States. What are they doing? Why, you cannot walk down a street in Washington without meeting them. We have a small standing army in Washington, and we purchased big locations for them. They say, "When in Rome, do as the Romans do." I suppose it would be, "When in Washington, do as the Americans do." They have spent money like water on this publicity and information campaign. In my opinion the good it has done has not amounted to a snap of the fingers, so far as educating the people of the United States is concerned, or to win the war. Our soldiers and the glorious work in Italy, Sicily, Africa and other places have done more than any information bureaux, past, present and future.
I believe in putting on the brakes, so far as these expenditures are concerned. The expenditures of this particular department are going up by leaps and bounds. Away back on July 13, 1943, it was a different story. They had no office. I have no quarrel with the parliamentary assistant, because he is a most excellent gentleman, and one whom I have known for a long time. But there is a difference of opinion between him and me and between the Prime Minister and me in respect of public matters like this one. The Prime Minister has done a great deal in the United States to bring about good will. I admit that; I give him credit for it. He is well liked over there. But I have differed with him on many public questions, and I do in this instance. I do not take anything back in what I have said. I was opposed to this proposition of a wartime information office, right from the start.

This branch has been under the control of almost half a dozen ministers and acting ministers. One of the ministers was a gentleman who went to the bench-a very good citizen. He had charge of this board at one time. Then it came into the hands of a new minister.
What do we find here? We find a number of newspaper men coming forward, and offices were opened in the United States in October, 1942. The office had been open for only ten months when the last vote was before the house. At page 4711 of Hansard for 1943 we find a description of policy. It is said that the men in New York and Washington work hard. They go down and look at these glorious offices, fitted out in New York city. Well, you would think that the field of the cloth of gold could not be compared with some of that furniture. One would be reminded of another place in this building, where he sees that kind of furniture. Then those men go to work, and they want to open offices also in San Francisco, Chicago and other places to educate America. Last year the parliamentary assistant said, as reported at page 4711 of Hansard:
Those suggested to me now are the representatives of the Associated Press, the Chicago Sun, the New York Daily News, the NFA service and a good many others.
After you have gone through all this, what do you find? Well, you find that there was a debate on this very question, namely, that of understanding Canada, which took place in the senate and house of representatives at Washington. What did they say? Some congressmen said that Canada to-day was paying tribute and cash taxes to Britain yet, the same as in the days of Lord North-a tribute of millions of pounds a year, in taxes taken out of this country by the imperial government. Then there was a debate in Washington on what was known as the Connolly bill-Senator Connolly who was in Ottawa last summer to attend a meeting of the empire parliamentary association. On that occasion he made a fine address. It was asked whether Great Britain should have five seats in a proposed new organization, or only one seat.
Mr. Denys Smith, writing in the May issue of the National Review, criticizes this policy. He states:
The similarity of American and British history, however, is not only unrecognized in the United States, but American information about the British empire appears to have become crystallized about fifty years ago so *far as the vast majority of the population is concerned. Some of the ideas entertained about modern Britain and the British empire would be a travesty of the truth were they applied to the days of George III. There are, unfoT-

War Appropriation-External Affairs
tunately, few ways of measuring the depth of this ignorance although it is manifest in every congressional debate on foreign policy and in many editorial disquisitions even in reputable newspapers. A recent Gallup poll showed that three-quarters of the population believed Canada paid taxes to the British treasury, an obvious residual impression left by the usual school textbook presentation of the war of independence as an attempt iby the parliament at Westminster, or as the textbook would more probably phrase it, the British king, to get taxes from the colonies for the benefit of the mother country. If there is that much ignorance about Canada, a country which is the United States closest neighbour and one which tens of thousands of Americans have visited at one time or another, there is small wonder at the ignorance displayed, say about India. British knowledge of America is far from perfect. But it is not as bad as American ignorance of Britain.
There is the same ignorance about Canada. I was glad to see the Prime Minister's efforts in collaborating with the great President of the United States and it is of the utmost importance that we continue to collaborate with our glorious ally to the south. But there is a right and a wrong way of approach. I have talked to a number of Americans. I was one of the officers of the municipality of Toronto for a great number of years; a large number of Americans visited that city in the summertime and I met many of them. They are very fine people, but they would respect Canada and the mother country more if they knew more about us, and if we would tell them the truth once in a while about our empire. There was a debate on foreign policy in both houses of congress three weeks ago last Monday, and the views expressed there were more significant than the general resolution passed in favour of post-war collaboration. There was a food convention at Atlantic City, a body known as the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration. It formulated its policy at a conference in Atlantic City, an American city which is typically American in the sense that its like would be hard to find elsewhere. The general Republican position toward world affairs combines two apparently irreconcilable concepts. First there is the suspicion of anything in the nature of a close association with a few powers in the post-war world, and a preference for an all-inclusive union of all countries large and small. Yet at the same time there is opposition to the principle of equal rights for all countries great and small. In other words, as to isolation they are back to the days of George Washington and Andrew Jackson- a policy of no commitments.
There was a chance, right in the cities of Washington, New York and Atlantic City, for our publicity men and this information bureau to act and do some good work, to educate the people of the United States. We
have a small standing army of publicity men and our military forces and other agents there. If they were to march down Bank street four abreast they would reach from here to Lansdowne park, but apparently no effort is made to explain the position of Canada to the people of the United States. Look at the glorious record which our Canadian soldiers have won in Europe, by their work in Sicily and in Italy, by their march across the desert, and by the capture of Rome. In every theatre of war they have distinguished themselves. But all that is not publicized in the United States by our publicity men.
There has been a wide expansion of the information bureau since last July. We had a debate in this house on July 12 last on the wartime information board, which continued on July 13 and lasted into the 14th and what have been the results from the efforts of our publicity bureau? What have we got? They have not been telling the people of the United States about Canada and what it has done. No one can justify the way in which our public relations officers and publicity men and the information bureau have expanded in numbers in the United States.
I have a return here which was brought down in accordance with an order of the house last week showing that we have 396 publicity officers, 156 of them being press agents and liaison officers in one branch alone. All these officers are to educate the public, mostly in the United States. It is really usurping the power of the press of this country and shows a lack of confidence in the press to establish such a board. A true picture should be given to the electors of what is happening at home and abroad. These public relations officers have expanded to a small regiment. Their work is not merely to educate the public but apparently to put before the public all that there is in Webster's dictionary. They tell us all about food, all about clothing, all about departmental policies. They have a spokesman in each department who gives interviews to the newspapers along the lines I have mentioned. Then they have what is called an apology department, a chief apologist for policy, past, present and future. He is really a ghost writer behind the scenes, a spokesman for this, that and the other department. There are 156 of these publicity, press and liaison officers, and I do not know how many there are altogether. That was never intended when the board was created. Then they get up Gallup polls to show what the state of public opinion is on various matters that come before the country. I believe that the information board has left undone what it should have done. When the
3588	COMMONS
War Appropriation-External Affairs
United States was losing ships through U-boat attack in the north Atlantic a great American general, Eisenhower, wrote to the head of Eire, de Valera, a strong letter telling what was happening to American ships and how the sinkings and the deaths of sailors were aiding the axis powers, and speaking of the policy with respect to southern Ireland. Why did we not do the same thing, and why did our information board not do the same thing? Why did our information bureau not give the people of Canada the facts? We should have done it ourselves. This United States general wrote that an explanation should be demanded from southern Ireland as to why United States ships were being sunk for lack of bases in southern Ireland.
The information bureau should have said something about the strikes that are going on in war time. They put advertisements in United States magazines, monthlies and newspapers. Here is a recent editorial from Life. It i3 a criticism along the lines of what we were told by the hon. member for Greenwood and by the Prime Minister of Australia the other day, and by others, that we are losing the battle in the war on the home front. This editorial in Life says:
The home front, speaking generally, seems to have no comprehension of the historic role that it is being called upon to play. Hence, instead of pulling together it is breaking apart. Thus in the last several months every major effort to stream-line the home front for war has failed. The farm bloc has scrambled a subsidy programme for keeping down the cost of living. In three of the most vital industries-coal, railroads and steel-labour has defied the government and driven wages upward. Efforts to tax the swollen war incomes that the nation is enjoying have wholly failed.
I believe in having a proper information bureau which will tell the people the facts, whether they are good, bad or indifferent. No matter how bad they are, and how bad the news is, the public should be informed. The policy of the government in expanding this service all over the United States, sending out a small expeditionary force of publicists, and gathering in all these correspondents, is not worth a snap of the fingers as regards helping the war along or educating America. Our brave soldiers, sailors and airmen will do Canada more good with the achievements which stand to their credit than all this expenditure of money upon advertisements in United States newspapers, and things of that kind. If we want to promote this sort of education let us do it in the British empire, because charity begins at home, and dear knows you have something to speak about in the glorious record which this empire has made in the war. Britain held the gate of the continent until [Mr. Church.1
our troops came to the aid of the motherland.
I hope there will be some retrenchment in this expenditure. Personally I would not continue it any longer, in view of the invasion now in progress. From the time of Lord North, nearly two hundred years, Britain has tried this kind of appeasement policy of spending money to educate America and the world at large, and it cannot be done. The glorious record of our soldiers in this war, the great achievements of the United* States army and navy, and the comradeship which this war has brought about between the forces of the United States, Canada and the mother country, will be of more lasting value than all the spending of money on newspaper advertising and other such material aids. '

Would the parliamentary
assistant kindly give the list of all the publications that are not mimeographed and that are not published by the king's printer? subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
There are other ways to
publicize the deeds of our heroes and have them publicized beyond Canada. One has only not be be fearful, to be above criticism, to be sure of his facts and to lose no opportunity to bring before the world the importance of the Canadian war effort. Sometimes the method which is used may be regarded as unorthodox, but if the results are good there will be nothing to complain about.
For instance, during a broadcast from London Mr. Churchill mentioned the achievements of other countries, but without mentioning Canada. The matter was brought before the house by the hon. member for Temis-couata who received some letters that were written in an unfriendly spirit by people who live in this country and who have not the right to call themselves Canadians, while on the other hand he received from Great Britain letters that would put those people to shame. To show you, Mr. Chairman, what could be done to publicize the war effort of Canada without any cost to this country, I will read
two letters that I have received, one from Montreal and one from Birmingham, England. The one from Montreal is as follows:
6400 Prince Arthur St. West, Montreal,
April 1, 1944.
Hon. Mr. J. F. Pouliot (L. Temiscouata),
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Dear Sir: I have read with surprise an article published in to-day's Gazette under the caption "Pouliot Claims Canada Slighted by Churchill" and 'having reference to Mr. Churchill's broadcast of last Sunday.
Now sir, for you to assume that Mr. Churchill slighted Canada you are taking a lot on yourself and I suggest that his words and snub to those who have nothing better to do at a time like the present, than to belittle the government or to embarrass them in their mighty task, might wiifli equal meaning and truth apply to you. Mr. Churchill happened to be speaking about the Japanese area in particular and the deliverance of Australia by American, Australian and New Zealand troops in particular reference to the Pacific area.
Why is it that you and people like you are always wanting to be "patted on the back"? I am quite sure that Mr. Churchill never for one moment had the slightest intention of doing what you accuse him of-
I did not accuse Mr. Churchill at all.
-for he has repeatedly spoken of and expressed his admiration for the part Canada has and is playing in the war effort, by men, money and materials. Surely it is not necessary that he should repeat this on every broadcast he makes. Mr. Churchill is far too wise, too big and too generous a man to do anything in the way of slighting any of the allied nations, and I submit, sir, that you are "all wet" in thinking and speaking otherwise. I hope you will think twice before you again make such regrettable speeches about one who has been simply marvellous in carrying the supreme load in this war. He deserves the wholehearted support and thanks of every right-thinking person in the allied cause. Such remarks as those attributed to you, sir, are grossly unfair and uncalled for, and by such you certainly are not helping the cause of Canada in an "all-out war effort."
I submit that where the censor is really necessary at times is within the house, when speeches like that reported as coming from you are made.
Yours truly,
Hubert G. Harris.
This is a man who has not the Canadian spirit. Now I will read a letter received from Birmingham from a true Englishman, one who represents the feeling of the British nation and who is different from this Mr. Harris:
2/212 Heneage St.,
Mr. Pouliot.
Dear Sir: Please do not think me presumptuous. But do you know that I said to my wife when listening to Mr. Churchill's talk-
And mark you, sir, this comes from Birmingham, England.

Birmingham,
, England.



War Appropriation-External Affairs
-that I should have thought so great a man would never have forgotten so splendid and courageous an ally as the good old Canadians. Personally I served with some of the gallant C.F.A. in the last war. So you can understand that I felt rather hurt they not being even mentioned. Still perhaps we must believe that in his case he just overlooked them. It does seem strange that I should see your remarks in one of our local newspapers, namely, the Birmingham Evening Dispatch of April 1, 1944, under the heading of "Little Dispatches." Now, dear sir, I do hope this little [bit of news will find you quite well and if it is not asking of you too much, to ask you to give my every good wish to Canada, God bless the hoys.
Yours very sincerely,
Sidney H. Clark,
late of the Royal Scots.
This is a letter I prize very much. It is a letter which is written not by a bloke but by a true Englishman. It did not cost the country anything. I do not pretend I see behind what was said of Canada at Westminster, but on the other hand every little bit helps, and it is the duty of members of parliament to lose no opportunity to show to the whole world what our country is doing for them. This is one item that has cost nothing. There is no bill for it.
But there is something else. The wartime information board is losing track of fundamentals and in preaching unity it creates disunity. I will explain that to you, sir, and you will understand me very well. In the first place, there is a mentality that has been created by the wartime information board to the effect that if we have no conscription it is to maintain national unity, because Quebec would resent it. On the other hand, no opportunity is lost to repeat over the radio and to publish in writing what the Minister of Labour has said in reply to me in the house, that the duty of every able-bodied Canadian of military age is to join the forces, leaving aside the idea and the suggestion of the essentiality of war industry in this country. I complain bitterly that the wartime information board has not taught the English-speaking provinces outside Quebec that what is accomplished by all men in essential industry is just as vital to the war effort as what is being done by the soldiers, and that without their assistance the soldier could not go anywhere. Was that ever published by the wartime information board? Never. It was the duty of that board to tell the Canadian people what they had to think in order to have a common thought regarding the war. Instead of that, inspiration has come from jingoes and junkers who showed no charity toward the province of Quebec but left the English-speaking people of Canada under the false impression that the people of Quebec were not doing their duty.

That was a great mistake on the part of the wartime information board and I cannot conceive that all the gentlemen who are working there, 393 besides stenographers, did not understand it. The question is obvious. It is that . if we accept the views of those jingoes and junkers the ideal Canadian soldier will be one who will walk on the land without clothes, without shoes, without arms, without ammunition, walk to the shore, swim across the ocean, pick up some stones in Ireland and fight the Germans with them. That is the ideal soldier in the minds of the jingoes and junkers.
The wartime information board has been remiss in its duty in telling the Canadian people about the importance of the work of the farmer, the fisherman and the man who is engaged in railroad occupations, the importance of all those who manufacture arms and ammunition and those who build boats. All those men deserve well from their country.
In the view of the jingoes and junkers the only man who serves his country well is the man who volunteers. I have no objection at all to praising the soldiers and giving them their due. They are good men. Canadians are such good soldiers that they are considered the best of all, and as Lord Mottistone said four years ago, they are now the spearhead of the army; not only was that so in Italy but it is so in France to-day. The Canadians, after having liberated His Holiness the Pope will deliver France from the enemy. But if they did not have behind them the man who is engaged in an essential occupation, and if those who have accomplished so much in essential occupations were not paid by the Canadian citizens who do not work actually in an essential industry but accomplish the important task of being taxpayers, where would the Canadian army be now? That has to be said. The Canadian people, especially the English-speaking Canadians have to be told that, and who could tell them that better than the wartime information board? In the first place those who are on the board must understand it and, after having understood it, they should inform the people about it.
I complain of something else besides that. This is not a censorship board. The duty of the wartime information board is precisely to inform the Canadian people. How is it that the liaison officers of that board have infested the press gallery to prevent-my hon. friend is jumping in his seat. I will refer him to one who has been named by the hon. member for St. Paul's already. They were there to tell the newspaper men that it was their duty not to publish reports of what had been said in parliament, what the people of Canada had

War Appropriation-External Affairs
a right to know; and that has been done. They have sinned not only by omission but by commission. That was done.
In my view, sir, the best thing to do with this item is to reduce it to one dollar and give it to the poor, and then give some freedom to the press. If the reports of the Canadian Press and the British United Press were published integrally by the Canadian newspapers they would be well informed. If the reports that are written by the journalists to their papers for the information of the readers were published integrally we would not need the wartime information board. I have nothing against those people. They mean well; and I will not say that the accomplishment of the board was to try to work out some kind of political propaganda. I will not go as far as that, but I will say that they have contributed more than any other body to destroy Canadian feeling in the hearts of Canadian people; they have contributed more than any other body to cause national disunity in Canada, to represent the province of Quebec in false colours; and they never had the courage to tell the Canadian people the truth about the nobility and the essentiality of the work of the farmers, railwayman, fishermen, the man who makes ammunition, arms and so on. That has never been done. Is it too late? I do not know. It is never too late to do good. I may be told that I am not a good Canadian because I express my views sincerely in this chamber. But, sir, at election time the farmers will be praised on every husting. Why is it not done now from the broadcasting studios of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the wartime information board? How is it that railwaymen are now considered as doing work that is not essential? They are told to join the army, even though they have had long railroad experience. They are told that by the wartime information board. That is to inform the Canadian people wrongly. That is what happens. We are coming to fundamentals. There are fundamentals that no one has the right to ignore, least of all the wartime information board. How long will it take to teach them fundamentals, to teach them the AJB.C.'s of national unity in Canada? After having led people in error, perhaps not always directly, but through insinuation, insinuation in which the province of Quebec was always the sufferer, why does the wartime information board not tell the Canadian people that the province of Quebec was high .up in the victory loan-in the victory loans, I should say-that the objective was attained there, to use Major Triquet's expression, sooner than anywhere else; that 100-226J
the French-Canadians of Quebec as well as their English-speaking fellow citizens are doing very well for the war effort. I could say the same thing of all those who belong to other races and who live in the province of Quebec. They are doing very well. Is it necessary for us to repeat it? I should not have to say that. It should have been said a long time ago by the wartime information board. It should not only have been said in this chamber but have been broadcast from ocean to ocean, so that no Canadian citizen, no Canadian woman, no Canadian child should ignore what has been done in the war by every part of this country.
Now, sir, that being said, I do not despair. I have said some truths, and I regret that the wartime information board until now has not come up to the standard we expected. It may improve; I hope it will, because there is plenty of room for progress.
My concluding words would be these. There is only one way to follow; that is the straight way. The duty of each board, whatever it is, under whatever minister, should not be to try to please or to displease; it should be to da what is right. What is essential in this country is national unity, but we shall attain it only if the same things are said to all parts of. Canada. I am opposed to special programmes-for the English-speaking provinces and other special programmes for the province of Quebec or over the French network. All French and English-speaking people, all Jews and all others in Canada should' be told the same thing. They should be told the truth about each other. When that is done we shall have national unity in Canada, and we shall realize that even, though there may be a handful of intriguers, in this country the mass of the people, whether English or French, are the very best.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I think I should say something in reply to the hon. member for Broadview and the hon. member for Temiseouata. Thp fact that they agree on a point does not mean necessarily that the point is either right or wrong, though I must say it is helpful in coming to a conclusion.
The hon. member for Temiseouata made a number of remarks with which I think I should deal factually. He asked, why the wartime information board1 did not say that Quebec had done well in the war loan. The wartime information board does not give news to the public at first hand; that is done by the press of Canada. It is not part of the work of the wartime information board to take over any of; the work of the press, and the publicity for the national war loans is in the hands of the national war finance committee. While the
3592	COMMONS
War Appi opriation-External. Affairs
wartime information, board ig glad to assist with secondary information, and to assist in seeing that information is given to the public, it does not issue the information about war loans in the first place. However, I think it will be found1 that the publications of the wartime information board in regard to the standing and contribution of Canadians to the war loans have done adequate justice to all parts of Canada including Quebec.
The hon. member spoke about the freedom of the press, and said how desirable it was that the press of Canada should be free. I think I can say in this house that the press of Canada is freer than the press of any other country in the world to-day. Never has the wartime information board either infested the press gallery, as suggested by my hon. friend, or done anything else in connection with the press except to help it in ways that the press desired. That is the function of the board.
Then the hon. member said that we had 396 'employees, not to speak of the stenographers. I do not know where he got the figure, but the number of employees of the wartime nforma-tion board is 157, including all the stenographers, office boys and everyone else.
The hon. member said that it was the duty of the board to assist in the education of the 'Canadian people and to tell them what to think. I deny, Mr. Chairman, that this is the duty of the board, or any other board, in a democratic country. Our people do not want to be told what to think. On the other hand it is the duty of the board to help the press and all other agencies that disseminate information throughout the country to give the people all the facts and all the information on which they can make up their own minds. That and nothing else is the function of the board. We have not done anything else; no one can say that we have done anything else; no one has brought forward a single fact or a single act that would support any such statement. The board is here to serve the people of Canada; it has no other duty. It serves them by giving them, principally through the agencies that deal directly with the public, all the facts and information on which people can make up their minds on the complicated questions as to which people have to make up their minds today. They are not easy questions, as we in this house know very well. It is our job in this house, as it is the job of the press, of the radio and, to some slight extent, of the wartime information board, to facilitate that process, but that is all the board can do. Let no one say that it is our job to tell the people what to think, because then we shall have lost this war.
{Mr. Claxton.]
Then the hon. member said that we had done nothing to make it clear that the jobs of the people back home, of the men working on the farms, of the men working in the factories, were just as vital as the job of the men fighting on the beacheads in France to-day. I deny that the job we are doing here in this parliament or in our factories or on our farms is just as vital as the job being done by those men who are offering their lives in France for our freedom to-day. I deny that. However, I do say that if you want a comprehensive picture of what the whole Canadian people are doing, either in the armed forces or on the farms or in the factories, look at "Canada at War" for March, or the French issue, "Le Canada en Guerre", and turn to pages 40 to 78. There you will find a picture of Canada at war at home. Pages 1 to 40 are devoted to Canada at war in the fighting services. If that is not a fair division of space in the sense desired by the hon. member for Temiscouata, I should like to know what is. If it errs on any side it does so in giving overemphasis to the fighting at home, but there are particular reasons for that. Statistically it requires more pages to picture the war at home and to break it down into significant figures.
Then the hon. member said that he wanted the names, occupations and salaries of the staff working for 'the wartime information board. Well, Mr. Chairman, 1 could take up the time of this committee by giving that information, if it were required; I have it here. There is no secret about it; it is available to any hon. member who wants to come and see it. However, all these details were given in a return brought down in the house on February 24. The information was complete up to that date, and I could go on from there and enlarge on it if the committee desired me to do so. I do not think hon. members would want me to take the time to do that, however; but if the hon. member for Temiscouata desires the facts and figures, he can get them either now or at any subsequent time.
The hon. gentleman also asked for particulars of any publications not placed through the king's printer. On inquiry I find that no publications are printed except through orders placed with the king's printer. In the case of a publication like this, "Canada at War", the king's printer obviously has to go outside the establishment on Sussex street because he has not a rotogravure press, but he lets that work in accordance wTith the ordinary practice, over which we have no control whatever. All the printed publications of the wartime information board are placed through the king's printer or printed by the king's printer.

War Appropriation-External Affairs
I thought the hon. member for Broadview made some rather helpful remarks. He suggested that we had not been doing a good enough job in informing the people of the United States as to Canada's war effort. The hon. member pointed out that we were failing in certain respects
Almost all the comments ever made with respect to the operations of the board can be categorized under two headings, either that we are not doing enough, or that we are engaging in political propaganda If one were to try to pick out the number of illustrations where any member has said that anything has been done wrong, he could number them on the fingers of one hand. He would not find more than five. The comment falls into one of two categories, either that we have not been doing enough, or that we are doing too much by way of teaching political propaganda.
In respect of not doing anything, I think all parties in the house at one time or another have expressed themselves to the effect that Canada should do more to make her war effort known, not only to the people of Canada but to the people of the United States, Great Britain, and those of other allied nations. All parties have said that, and the board has tried to carry out that idea. Within its resources I say it has done so, admirably. The hon. member for Broadview suggested that to-night.
If I might refer back to what happened in a previous session, I would direct the attention of the committee to a question asked by the hon. member for Parkdale on November 4, 1941. That question, as reported at page 4059 of Hansard of that year was as follows:
In view of the importance of having Canada's war effort more widely known in the United States than it is at present, will the Prime Minister tell the house whether it is the government's intention at an early date to establish a Canadian bureau of information in New York?
Then, in the debate last year the hon. member for Lake Centre said that "there is still room for greater endeavours in the furnishing of information to the United States."
We have endeavoured to carry out this injunction, and have had a great deal of support from the press and people of Canada, of the United States and of Great Britain. At this point may I pay tribute to the number of Americans who have voluntarily given their time and services, completely free, by way of radio programmes, moving pictures and personal appearances to help make the cause of Canada better known not only in the United States but in Canada.
Our wartime information, board is attacked on another count, namely, that of being an
instrument of government propaganda. That is the kind of charge made by every opposition in every democratic parliament-and I suppose it is quite natural that it should be made.
But in this instance no one has brought forward a single word, a single note or a single line of justification for the charge. They have been generalities-the kind of generalities which get headlines in the favourable press.
I should like to be perfectly frank with the committee. The facts and figures in connection with the operation of the wartime information board are open to any member. Any member who has gone to the general manager, Mr. A. D. Dunton, who has succeeded Mr. Grierson, has got any information he wanted. He can get anything he likes. The facts and figures are available to him, and to anyone else in a position of authority similar to that held by hon. members.
Men have come from the press to the office in Washington, the office in New York or the office in Ottawa. They have looked into the operations of the board and have ended up by saying, "How can we help? This is an important job." That is the kind of attitude I hope hon. members will take with regard to this activity. There has been no evidence or no statement to bear out the suggestion that there has been anything in the nature of political propaganda issued from the office of the wartime information board, from beginning to end. It issues hundreds of pages of material. It also makes arrangements with radio programmes, with editors and with writers. Hon members will have noticed a steady increase in the attention given to Canada in United States and British publications during the last two years. There has been a steady increase. I do not suggest that any one of those editors has been influenced jn any sense by the wartime information board. That would be quite improper. On the other hand I do suggest that those editors would not have had the material upon which they have based their articles, unless the wartime information board had helped them in a perfectly proper way.
Then, with regard to this charge of issuing propaganda may I call attention to the fact that the wartime information board is, in fact, a board. It is under the chairmanship of Mr. N. A. M. MacKenzie, president of the university of New Brunswick, who has now accepted a post as president of the university of British Columbia. The board consists chiefly of senior civil servants representing agencies which might be interested. That board would no more be a party to political propaganda than hon. members, who know

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I had hoped that the parliamentary assistant would give a somewhat more complete account of what the board is doing to inform the people of Canada at home and in the armed forces, and the people of other countries, including those of the United States, regarding Canada's war effort. I believe that a statement of that kind, setting before the committee something in greater detail of what is being done by the board, would be a valuable piece of information, not only for the board itself but for members of the committee.
I have no reason to believe that there is any considerable body of criticism from any part of the press on the ground that the board is usurping the place of the press in Canada. I have never heard that criticism expressed to any extent. In many parts of the country, however, I have heard commendations from small-town editors when they have spoken of the assistance the board has given them in providing information which was not readily accessible in any other way, and which they could pass on to their readers.
If the facts are as set out by the hon. member for Broadview, so far as a lack of knowledge of Canada's war effort on the part of our neighbours to the south is concerned, then I would suggest that his statement offers the best possible argument hon. members could find in favour of an extension of the type of work the board is doing. The work of the board is of such a nature that, I think we must all agree, it is difficult to assess its
*Mr. Claxton.]
value in dollars and cents. The work of the board is like all educational work in that its value cannot be measured in terms of money. No one will question the need of keeping the Canadian people well informed. I am sure that none of us feels that there is the slightest danger of our people becoming too well informed because of the work the board is doing.
I would suggest to the parliamentary assistant, who spoke a moment ago of the members and staff of the board going back to their former jobs when the war is over, that there is a very great need for work such as this board can do in Canada after the war is over. There is a dire need of some organization that will interpret one part of Canada to other parts of Canada, or each part to other parts. Canada is a vast country and we have many different points of view and many different interests. There is just as great a lack of knowledge on the part of Canadians in one section of the country regarding Canadians living in other sections, as there is on the part of United States citizens about Canada as a whole. I , would suggest that the board consider the possibility of undertaking the task of interpreting Canadians in each part of Canada to Canadians in other parts.
I suggested a year ago that there is in this country the need of certain books that can be used in the schools of the country, books that will interpret to the students attending school in the English-speaking provinces the life of the people of Quebec, and books that can be used in the schools of Quebec to interpret to the school children there the ways of life of the people in other provinces. I am satisfied that it would do much to cement the unity of Canada, of which the hon. member for Temis-couata has been speaking so much, and I know of no better organization to do that work when the war ends than some such organization as the wartime information board. Any contribution which the board is making either to inform our own people here, or to inform Canadian boys and girls in the armed forces about Canada's effort in this war, about conditions in Canada at the present time, about what is happening in Canada, is all to the good. Anything that I have heard from those in the forces or from those overseas is that they get all too little information about Canada, that the more information this board can give Canadians in the armed forces about what is happening in Canada to-day, the better.
Certainly no one will doubt the necessity and the value of informing our neighbours to the south about Canada. Such work cannot be valued in monetary terms. It will be of immeasurable value not only during the war

War Appropriation-External Affairs
but when the war is over. It will help to create a much better understanding between this country, the United States and other countries. Even though we have to achieve that at the price of giving the Liberal government credit for some of the things which it is doing, nevertheless, I think it is well worth doing. I do not see how in time of war you can tell the Canadian people or inform other people of what Canada is doing without at the same time giving credit to the government which has the responsibility for carrying on the war effort. I do not see how that can be avoided. I do think the government is obviously getting a good deal of advertising through the wartime informaton board, but I can see no way in which that can be avoided unless you are going to keep our people uninformed, and I do not think we should undertake to keep our people uninformed just because by informing them we are at the same time giving credit to a government.
I believe that without going into the field of political propaganda, particularly in keeping the boys in the armed forces informed about what is happening in Canada, the board could very well give information regarding what is being done by other parties as well as what is being done by the Liberal party. I do not think it is necessary to go into the field of active political propaganda, but if you are going to inform particularly the boys in the armed forces, I am sure that they are just as anxious to know what the Progressive Conservatives, the C.C.F. and other political parties in which they are interested are doing as they are to know what the government is doing.
Certainly I have no hesitation in supporting this estimate, even though it is increased largely over last year. From any knowledge that I have of the wartime information board, I would say that they are doing valuable work in the field of education both in Canada and in other countries.

If the hon. member will wait for a moment, I refer him to the series of mimeographed documents from the board which are coming to our desks right now dealing with post-war planning. As I said this afternoon, they are good. Every time one comes to my desk I send to the board for several additional copies because I know people who would like them. But I would remind the parliamentary assistant that with respect, for example, to post-war plans, all the plans the board has collected, though admittedly those of the government of the day, are the plans of one party, and I suggest that in giving out that information alone, the wartime information board is not fully informing the public as to what is going on in this country with respect to post-war planning. Not only the government but my hon. friends to the right, we in our group, and our hon. friends to the left are working out plans of a general nature with respect to the post-war period, and plans for the demobilization and rehabilitation of the members of the forces. It seems to me that, just from the point of view of giving informative material, the wartime information board should be collecting and making available this other information as well. I know that when I discussed the matter this afternoon it somehow got under the skin of the hon. member for York-Sunbury. To him it seemed like asking the wartime information board to use public money to put out political propaganda. Well, when one speaks of "political propaganda" in that tone of voice I agree with him, and the Prime Minister, and the parliamentary assistant, in saying that public money should not be used for that purpose; let there be no mistake about that. But there is all the difference in the world between political propaganda of the kind which is put out in an attempt to run down some other party and nothing more, and the straightforward1 presentation by responsible political parties of their platforms and of the things for which they stand.
Speaking again under the two headings, material for our people here at home, and material for the armed forces, I feel that the wartime information board is not doing its

War Appropriation-External Affairs
full job unless it collects for both groups the material of the various political parties who are trying to make their contribution to the advancement of Canadian life at this time. The parliamentary assistant, or the Prime Minister, who spoke on this matter for a moment or two about six o'clock, can point out that there is nothing political in what the board is putting out, that all the wartime information board is giving is a straight statement of facts as to what the government is doing. That is true, but from the very nature of the case it appears to redound to the credit of one party. I am not worried about that. So far as our group is concerned, as hon. members know, we spend a great deal of effort and energy and as much money as we can collect in putting out our own literature. I am not concerned about ourselves, but I am concerned about the wartime information board doing a proper job with public money and getting full and complete information to our people in this country and the members of the armed forces.
Despite what the parliamentary assistant has already said on this particular question tonight, I hope he will reconsider it. I hope that when this debate is over, members of the board, the non-partisan gentlemen whom he has described, in their next meeting will give this matter consideration and see whether there is not room in these mimeographed documents, in "Canadian Affairs", and in "Canada Digest", on the basis of supplying straight factual material, to give something of what other political parties are doing at the present time in their efforts, along with the Liberal party, which happens to be the government of the day, to make a contribution to the advancement of Canadian life.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
This vote is so insignificant in comparison with the item which has just been earned that I should like a lot of further information. I said nothing on the previous vote because I had not anything particular to say. I felt that the wartime information board had done under the circumstances a pretty fair job. Perhaps it could be better; perhaps it could be worse. But comparing the two votes, I cannot see why this one is so very small. We are going to win the war; I have not any doubt about that; but we have also to win the -peace. This vote refers to a committee on reconstruction. It will not be able to do very much on $25,000. What is it doing? As far as I know there are four different committees concerned with this subject, or three in addition to the parliamentary committee. The parliamentary committee has had before it many capable delegations and witnesses, and the chairman has sent to the house a statement, in my judgment of very great value, of what can be done to win the peace through rehabilitation and reconstruction. But this vote does not apply to the parliamentary committee, for as far as I know that committee has incurred little expenses, unless perhaps in bringing the odd witness from out of town. What has this committee done? Has it made any plans, and, if so, how could it make them for $25,000? Plans for work call for the services of engineers and surveyors, men qualified to prepare them, and others who are competent to make specifications, blueprints and details. Has this body done anything like that? If not, what has it done? I have read, of course, newspaper speeches here and there, but they do no-t mean a thing unless the plans and specifications of the jobs and the programmes which are to be carried out are

War Appropriation-External Affairs
prepared. Has this committee arranged for any such plans, specifications or programmes? If so, as far as I know they have not been tabled in the house.
One of the ministers said that plans and specifications were ready for programmes, while another minister said that plans and specifications for programmes are perhaps not necessary. I forget the exact words. Well, what has this committee prepared for postwar rehabilitation? The vote is a small one and I am not opposing it, but I want to know what the committee has been doing and what is ready. Few in this house have travelled in Canada more than I have in the last two or three years and I have not heard anywhere of anything being ready. If there is anything ready, why would every one of the provinces be setting up rehabilitation machinery of their own and going to a lot of expense. Ontario has set up a department and it is travelling around this country and the United States. What has this committee being doing? What has it really prepared, and what is actually ready which will give one man a job after the war?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
As hon. members know, the hon. member for Davenport has taken a keen interest in the work of rehabilitation and seeing that we are ready for the post-war situation. This vote is reduced from $47,250 last year to $25,435.08 this year. The difference is on account of the fact that the James advisory committee on reconstruction has concluded its work, been thanked by the government and passed out of existence. All its reports, including the reports of subcommittees, have been printed except the report of the subcommittee on housing, which should be printed in the next two weeks. The economic advisory committee to which this vote refers has since 1939 been advising the government on questions of economic policy. Since 1940 it has been advising the government on policies relative to reconstruction and full employment. That committee is still in existence and actively at work. It has a limited number of full-time people engaged by the committee itself on this work, but very largely it consists of senior civil servants and people drawn from other departments and paid by those other departments. That explains the fact that the vote is so small. A large proportion of the people working for the committee are paid by their permanent departments. I can give this committee the membership of the committee, but it is on the records available. The committee is advising the government on economic policy, particularly with reference to reconstruction.
iOO-227
The hon. member for Davenport asks, has it a single work ready? The answer is that that committee has not; that is not its function. That committee is advising the government on the kind of economic policies necessary to see that all the people of Canada, whether employed in industry or in farming or in the professions or other occupations, shall have the best possible opportunity of full employment after the war, and it is engaged in planning at that level. In addition, that committee has appointed a subcommittee and one or two officers who are endeavouring to coordinate all the planning of public works that is being carried on-and it is being carried on-by the government departments themselves on postwar works and projects, which is quite a different thing, though it is the kind of thing the hon. member for Davenport has particularly mentioned. These plans and projects for public works are being prepared and coordinated and the information with regard to them is being collected through that committee, so that the committee ties in to that work of planning post-war works and projects to be conducted by the federal government as part of its public works, although the committee is not charged with responsibility for carrying out these works itself. The works would be carried out by the departments concerned, such as the Department of Public Works, the Department of Fisheries, or the Department of Mines and Resources, or by some agency set up by them or by the provinces or by the municipalities, depending upon the arrangements to be worked out. The committee is endeavouring to collect and coordinate information on planning done in that field. I should answer my hon. friend in all frankness that the primary purpose of the committee is not to plan actual blueprints for any work but to advise the government on general policies with regard to reconstruction so as to bring about a maximum employment, maximum income and maximum security for the Canadian people.
Mr. MacNlOOL: I hope I did not say anything that in any way reflected on what the committee has done. I was under the impression when the committee was set up that it was to make preparations for after-war rehabilitation, to win the peace as well as the war, which is being won by the military. I have searched diligently and carefully, and I have inquired just as diligently, to find out if there is anything ready. I have said, and I do not hesitate to say again, that I remember distinctly what 'happened at the end of the last war. If there were any committees at that time preparing anything, I do not know, but if there were committees following the

last war, the fact is that there was nothing but chaos in regard to employment, I should not blame the government of that day because they had no experience to guide tihem. But this government has. It has the experience of the disastrous situation that followed the last war, and I have hoped right along, since the government set up three or four different committees, that something definite will be done in advance. speechtext: The intention is to set up a department of reconstruction and I agree with that. I believe that much good will come of a competent body headed by someone who is thoroughly qualified. We should have an able head of the reconstruction department. If we have, I look forward to its doing a good job. I may infer that the information gathered by this advisory committee to which the parliamentary assistant has referred will be turned over to the department of reconstruction rather than to mines and resources, although mines and resources has an opportunity to do much good work also. I want to feel that every member is sincere and earnest in seeing to it that the men who come back from this war will not have to go through what the boys went through who came back from the last war-not in a country where there are millions of opportunities. All we need to do is to get men who are big enough, who are thoroughly qualified and who understand the problems involved and can make the necessary lay-out. The parliamentary assistant has said that this vote is small because the particular committee is being wound up. I suppose we can only hope that the information it has compiled will be put in the hands of someone who will see to it that a programme is prepared against the day when the war ends. I am one of those who believe that it will end sooner than a good many people think. I have that much confidence in those who are running the war on our side. It may collapse earlier than we anticipate. I hope it does because, the sooner it does, the sooner will our gallant men come back and have a chance to build up the country. I hope everything will be ready for them to set to work and earn a living for themselves.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Aeronautics Act to provide for the establishment of an air transport board to perform the functions of a licensing and regulatory -body in respect of commercial air services and to advise the minister on matters connected therewith. Provision will be made by the said measure for the payment for services of the members of the board and the employment of necessary officers, clerks and employees.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Does the minister propose making a statement before going into committee or when we are in committee?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
The bill before the committee amends the Aeronautics Act of 1922 in order to give effect to the government's announced policy on domestic civil aviation. The discussion on that subject a few weeks ago covered the government's intention in that regard, and this amendment to the Aeronautics Act puts into force the policy announced at that time.
The effect of the amendments is to form a board of three, a chairman and two members, who will administer the Aeronautics Act, take over the duties now being performed by the board cf transport commissioners in regulating civil aviation as well as the duty of assigning air worthiness certificates and of licensing aviation enterprises within Canada. In addition, the board will function to advise the government as to ways and means of advancing civil aviation. The board will take the initiative in laying out routes, within Canada and overseas, which promise possibilities of profitable operation and will guide the government in seeing that these routes are operated by Canadians who are capable of carrying out such undertakings.
The judicial functions of the board are not new, but the functions of the board as advisers to the government on aviation policy are new, and will, I think, be helpful in bringing about the rapid development of civil aviation, both internal and external.
In general, the act follows the provisions of the Aeronautics Act of the United States. The functions of this board will be similar to
the functions of the civil aeronautics authority of the United States. I think detailed discussion should await second reading of the bill, when we shall have the amendments in detail before us, and when a more complete discussion of the purpose of the bill and the means of effecting that purpose can be arranged. In the meantime I shall be glad to answer any questions on the subject matter of the resolution that hon. members may wish to ask.

In the amendments proposed, _the minister means the Minister of Transport except for military matters, in which event the minister means the Minister of National Defence.
