Aeronautics Act

The control and supervision of the civil aviation branch of the Department of National Defence is hereby transferred from the Minister of National Defence to the Minister of Trans. port, and the said branch is hereby transferred from the Department of National Defence to the Department of Transport.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Then is the Minister of Transport to be the minister in charge under the Aeronautics Act as it is to be amended?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: A situation exists there which I have explained in the house once or twice already. When I was transferred from the ministry of transport to the ministry of munitions and supply, by arrangement with the then Minister of Transport and by direction of the Prime Minister, and by the exercise of the Transfer of Duties Act, the air services branch of the Department of Transport was transferred for administration to the Minister [DOT]of Munitions and Supply. That was done [DOT]because one of the important duties of the ministry of munitions and supply at that time was the building of airports. The air services branch of the Department of Transport had developed a highly skilled engineering personnel for the building of airports, and it was my feeling that the Department of Munitions and Supply should not be required to duplicate that personnel. It was and is the duty of the Minister of Munitions and Supply to construct the airports required by the armed services, and the practical way of bringing about an organization to do such work seemed to be to transfer the air services branch of the Department of Transport to the new ministry. Therefore the air sendees branch is administered at the present time by the Minister of Munitions and Supply.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Who will be administering the new act?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The Minister of Munitions and Supply, until the Transfer of Duties Act is again called upon to move it back to the *department from which it came.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Why is it necessary to go back to the Aeronautics Act and give the minister, who apparently now will be the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the very wide powers contained in that act? They are veiy much wider than the powers given to the transport board, as the minister knows. Why was it necessary to give such veiy wide powers as are contained in the Aeronautics Act?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
The powers contained in the Aeronautics Act are those required for the [DOT]control of civil aviation. The Department of Transport only exercised certain regulatory functions, but the Aeronautics Act covers a
[Mr Howe.]
great many matters that are not at present within the purview of the board of transport commissioners. That board is a judicial body, which simply interprets legislation, and does not initiate projects. It acts as a judicial body in connection with air matters.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Are the powers under the Aeronautics Act to be reduced?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The minister himself will have all the powers that are at present contained in the Aeronautics Act?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Is it the intention to have Trans-Canada Air Lines operated by the government under this act? As I see it, Trans-Canada Air Lines can be operated by the minister direct; that is what it amounts to.

Aeronautics Act

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Trans-Canada Air Lines has its own act. It operates under the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act. Its operations are subject to the regulations of the Aeronautics Act, just as the operations of any other service are subject to the Aeronautics Act.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Which takes precedence?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: That is provided for by the amendment. The Trans-Canada Air Lines Act provides for management for the Trans-Canada Air Lines. It also provides the manner in which it shall be assigned routes, and the limits governing its operation. I assume that the minister, under the Aeronautics Act, will confine his attention to such matters as are not covered by the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Then the situation will be that the Trans-Canada Air Lines will no longer be operated by Canadian National Railways, but will come under and be operated directly by the government.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: No, not at all. The only difference will be that the directors of Trans-Canada Air Lines will not be directors of the Canadian National Railways. It will be operated by a board of directors, just as the Canadian National Railways is operated by a board of directors. But the two will not be operated by the same board of directors.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Will the board of Trans-
Canada Air Lines be civil servants?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Or outsiders?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Yes, outsiders.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: But they will be very directly under the minister?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: No more so than the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: But if it is administered under this act it will be very directly under the minister. In effect, it makes the minister a dictator in respect of all the airways in Canada, does it not?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Perhaps so; but who would you
suggest should be dictator?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I do not think there should be a dictator, myself.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
This resolution is presented to the committee in a very awkward fashion. In the first place, the minister is to create a board just for the purpose of licensing and regulating. The present Minister of Munitions and Supply was formerly Minister of Transport. I very well remember when a board
such as he now proposes to appoint in respect of commercial aviation in Canada was appointed to regulate railways. In the first place the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada was set up. The organization is now known as the board of transport commissioners. At that time it was limited to railway rates. We have seen what it did with this country. That board did not regulate anything. It was a political board, and there was afterwards added to it control over express,, telephone companies and all that kind of thing. It was given wide jurisdiction.
I have looked into the original Aeronautics Act the minister now proposes to amend. This parliament will run into all kinds of damage suits if it proceeds with this measure, because I believe the amendment proposed to the statute law, as now suggested by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, is ultra vires of this parliament, and is confiscatory since bonds were sold of one aviation company. I should like to find out what the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada has had to say about this. Was he consulted in respect of this amendment? Or was this matter looked into by the lawyers for. Trans-Canada Air Lines-the minister's own lawyers? Were they, the legal people who drafted this resolution,, which proposes an amendment?
I protest against the measure. We are now in the seventy-second day of the session. It is hopeless for the minister to think he can have an act of parliament passed through like this, one which upsets the whole policy of the country in regard to civil aviation. The proposal for civil aviation would involve millions of dollars, and it will interfere with the rights, the functions, the statutory privileges and property rights of two other large railway corporations. It is practically confiscatory. That is my opinion with respect to the proposed bill to set up the board.
Why does a minister of the crown need a board to advise him as to the way to arrange licences and regulations? Is a minister of the crown not responsible to parliament?' Under our parliamentary system of government, is he not responsible to the country? Is he not responsible to the people for the very large expenditures which are to be made? This is a leap in the dark. This whole programme and policy of civil aviation proposed by the minister, and this regulatory board',, do not commend themselves to the wisdom and judgment of the people of Canada.
We had a long debate on this matter only a month ago. Now we have before us a resolution, to be followed by a bill. I do not believe parliament has power to pass such legislation in its present form. If we do, we shall get

Aeronautics Act
into all kinds of trouble, because we cannot have what we call freedom of the air under a regulatory body such as this. Here we have a minister of the crown, asking parliament to pass a resolution on which a bill is to be founded setting up a regulatory board, which will also advise on licences, with powers which no minister of the crown can have, .under our constitution.
Not only is this wrong, from the point of view of law, but it is bad public policy. This was never attempted before. A board is to be set up, and it is to have supervision over a minister of the crown in respect of the expenditure of money allocated to his department. It will have power over functions which he would have, under our constitution. We are taking a leap in the dark. It will lead to all kinds of trouble. Certainly it is not in the interests of civil aviation. I believe it will sound the death knell of civil aviation.
More than a year has passed since April 2, 1943, and in that time nothing has been done. To-day a report was withdrawn by the hon. member for St. Boniface, as chairman of the select committee on railways and shipping. They went into matters connected with Trans-*Canada Air Lines and the policy herein of the minister. An inquiry was conducted, and questions were asked. I was surprised to note what was done this afternoon. We saw that the -report of the committee was presented; as a matter of fact it was presented last Friday. There was reference made in that report to the policy contained in this resolution, namely, that of civil aviation. There was further reference to licensing, and all that kind of thing.
Then the chairman of the committee rose in his place this afternoon and, all of a sudden, withdrew his report. What was his reason for doing that? Because the report would have to be discussed' before this resolution could come up. Under the rules of the house with respect to anticipation it could not be accepted, when this resolution was to be introduced, and when there was to be a discussion as to the setting up of a regulatory body with powers to issue licences, and all that kind of thing.
I must confess I cannot understand it, and I never saw that procedure before. The committee was to go over these expenditures of the Canadian National Railways, and affiliated bodies, including Trans-Canada Air Lines. It did that. Witnesses were examined, and there was a good deal of the hallelujah chorus in the committee about what a wonderful system they had. Yet when one of our own ministers wanted to go across to the continent we had to go to Washington and get a Liberator.
(Mr. Church.]
Civil aviation is only in its infancy in Canada. I have been before the board of railway commissioners many times in the past and also before the beard of transport commissioners. I have appeared in connection with telephone rates, freight rates, passenger rates and express rates. They never regulate anything. The applicant always gets what he asks for, with interest. And this particular board will be nothing but a board of moonshine. It will appoint a lot of officers and servants and agents and other people-to do what?-to help strangle the movement. I hope the committee will stop, look and listen before the minister is permitted to make this step. I can say this: I really believe he is wrong. He is wrong in policy; he is wrong in principle; he is wrong in the law. It is going to mean confiscatory legislation with respect to a very fine transportation company which has borne the burden and heat of the day. As I said a month ago when this matter was up, I think it should be sent to a committee of the house where the minister's policy could be thoroughly considered and everybody concerned given a hearing.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
If I might answer that point, we are doing in connection with aviation exactly what the private radio stations have been asking the government to do in connection wtih control of the air waves. The private stations object to the C.B.C. operating a chain of radio stations and at the same time controlling the private industry. I might point out that the board we are discussing to-night is not an operating board. Trans-Canada Air Lines has an operating board, but it has no regulative authority, and is itself subject to the regulations of the aeronautics board. This is exactly the situation which the private radio stations have been seeking in connection with the air waves.
I am getting attacked from various angles to-night. The hon. member for Vancouver South claims that the minister has too much authority, and the hon. member for Broadview suggests that the minister is divesting himself of his authority in favour of the board. I think this amendment involves no great change in governmental responsibility for the administration of aviation in Canada.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I am afraid that there is.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: No change whatever.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I agree with the statement which the minister made when this resolution first reached the committee stage, to the effect that we could discuss the subject much better when the bill is before us. I rose to ask him just one question, but now that I am on my feet it might not be out of place for me to come to his defence a little because he is being attacked by our hon. friends to my right and he does not seem to have many supporters to help him out.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: You both need a lot of them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The minister and I frequently disagree in matters of policy, and even with respect to this bill there are tome criticisms which I expect to be making. But in the main I feel that the minister and the government are moving in the right direction when they seek to establish public control over so important a phase of our national life to-day as civil aviation.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Now I am beginning to suspect the legislation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I hope that my support of the measure will not be responsible for its being defeated by the minister's own supporters. At any rate, I repeat that every step that is taken by any government to establish public control over a matter so important as aviation will have our unqualified support. A few minutes ago when this feature of the bill was being revealed, one hon. member to my right suggested that it would mean a government monopoly, and I think he even used the word "dictatorship." I resent that language being used as descriptive of public control. In this day and age there are many instances of concentration of power.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: And many concentration camps.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The minister realizes, in introducing this bill, that in certain instances where there is a concentration of power there is only one thing to do, namely, to place that power in the hands of the people, and in the sense in which this bill proposes to do that with respect to civil aviation it has our support.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: If you lived in British Columbia you would not be so keen on public control.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Does the hon. member not support this measure?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I do not know yet; I am not sure. I have an open mind.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: There have not been many Liberal supporters of this measure, and that is why we come to the assistance of the minister.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Actually I do not think
he appreciates it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
We shall be able to discuss the various points when the bill is before us, but I have one question. The minister stated earlier this evening that the board to be set up would in some respects be similar to the United States civil aeronautics board. He referred to the act under which that board functions when he spoke on this subject on March 17 of this year, and referred to the fact that the United States civil aeronautics act-I am looking at page 1573 of Hansard- provides that no common carrier (that is, surface carrier) shall own, manage, or operate any air carrier. He made that reference immediately after pointing out that it was the intention of the government to provide that the railways should divest themselves of ownership of airlines. May I ask him whether he can indicate at this time that this bill will give effect to that principle particularly with respect to the proposed divorce between the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and Canadian Pacific Air Lines?
Aeronautics Act

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The bill provides that there shall be no common ownership of surface carriers and air carriers.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: In what way is the new board, the air transport board, subject to the minister? What is the tie between the minister and the air transport board?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The minister is responsible for the administration of civil aviation in Canada. The board has certain judicial functions in its own right, and can decide certain judicial matters.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Would their judicial functions be within the control of the minister, or separate from the minister?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
The judicial functions are
directly under the control of the board, except that in certain cases there is an appeal to the minister. But the government is not attempting to divest itself of its responsibility for administering civil aviation. The government's experience, and my own, are wholly against an attempt of that sort. We had a perfect example of that in 1932, when the Conservative government of that day undertook to divest itself of responsibility for the administration of the Canadian National Railways. It set up a trusteeship of three men to administer the property, and by 1936, when the trusteeship was dissolved, it needed about one or two more years to make it a trusteeship in bankruptcy. The road was rapidly heading that way. The government at that time again assumed its responsibilities for the railway, and the-

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Was that not a condition of the times rather than a condition of the set-up?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Perhaps each contributed.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: It is not a comparison.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
I could mention, if I were
not getting fairly close to home, other examples where a government has tried to divest itself of responsibility, without success to the government or prosperity to the object.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
We might go near home
on that, eh?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Yes. So that we shall not discuss that. Nevertheless this government believes in government responsibility for government operations, and the amendments proposed to the act are not inconsistent with that belief.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
In other words, the air
transport board is to be directly under the minister?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Correct.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
The minister said that that, as I understand it, was not the position of the board of transport commissioners.
' Mr. HOWE:	That is correct, yes. The
board of transport commissioners is a judicial body equivalent to a court, and its duty is to administer an act. That board has no function beyond the administration of the act -a wholly judicial function. This is a board which is both judicial and advisory.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
In other words, the board
of transport commissioners had to decide whether an applicant for a licence should get the licence, on certain well-defined principles, which might be summed up as public convenience and necessity, and it had also to follow certain judicial principles in deciding what tolls would be charged.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: As I understand it, this new transport board .will no longer be subject to-those stipulations; it will no longer have to-decide on the basis of public convenience and necessity whether or not a licence should be granted?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The jurisdiction is set out in-the bill. I think if my hon. friend will delay this discussion until he sees the bill he will' find that his fears in that regard are unnecessary.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: But in effect now the minister is over and above that air transport board?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Not in judicial matters.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
While he was not over and
above the board of transport commissioners? Is that not so?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
I might point out that the
board has two sets of functions. One is purely judicial; that is, when deciding matters of fact the board will be governed by the act; in that case the minister has no right to overrule them, except in the event of an appeal.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: If I may interrupt, that is what I wanted to ask the minister. After the board has ruled on a judicial matter, is there a right of appeal to the minister or to some other body?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
There is the right of appeal to the minister on certain matters, not all matters, but certain matters where there is an element of judgment as well as an element of judicial decision in interpreting the law. In i certain limited matters there is provision for an appeal to the minister. Ordinarily, in

Aeronautics Act
judicial matters the board is bound by the
act and its decision is final. However, the board will also initiate air projects. The j board of transport commissioners is not an initiating board. This board can initiate plans, and present them to the government for execution, and that, I anticipate, will be a very important part of the work of the board. That is the purpose in having a board whose interest is entirely that of aviation, and whose important task will be to develop ; for Canada a well thought out, well conceived system of aviation.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Would it not be wise to maintain some board that did act in a judicial manner-

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: This board does. I have explained that point several times.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: -and let perhaps some department of government do the advising and : initiating, rather than try to make the board sit on both sides of the fence at once? It does not seem to me as though those two functions can be carried opt by the one body. The minister may be able to solve that in some way or another. How does he propose to get around that difficulty?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Has not the board of transport now got those two functions?
1 Mr. GREEN: No. The board of transport commissioners has far more independence in 1 deciding on applications than this air trans' port board will have.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I will agree that the board of transport commissioners is an entirely independent body, but I point out that its duty is wholly negative. It initiates nothing. If an application comes before the board, it determines whether the application complies with the Transport Act, or whether it does not. If such application does comply with the act it is approved; if it does not it is rejected. I point out that this new board has judicial functions in a similar way.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: On the same principles as are set out in the Transport Act?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
The hon. member had better wait for the bill to determine that. The principles are set out in the bill. They are varied in some particulars. The new board also has the function of attempting to build as well as J to regulate. Civil aviation in the United States, which is more highly developed than in any other country, has been developed by a board of this type, and, I believe, developed admirably. I think that by and large the air transport system of the United States is a very successful development, and that its
civil aeronautics authority has contributed much toward that fortunate situation. I believe it is a model -which Canada can very well follow.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Of course, there the government does not operate the air lines, does it?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Trans-Canada Air Lines is just another air line as far as the air transport board is concerned. There is no connection between the two, except that the air transport board has regulatory functions over Trans-Canada Air Lines.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Over the CJP.R.?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Over every air line and every plane that carries passengers.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The Trans-Canada Air Lines will now be more directly under the board than before.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: It is not in the same position as the United States, and it is in the same position as radio in Canada to-day. The board has not at all the same functions as the board of transport commissioners. The board of transport commissioners have decisions to make as between the government-owned railways and the privately-owned railways and all the way through, as to whether the privately-owned railways should put a line in a certain place or whether it should be done by the government-owned1 railways. This board will not have any judicial function at all; and wherever privately-owned air lines are concerned, where they start to interfere with Trans-Canada Air Lines, the board will decide against the privately-owned air lines and in favour of the government-owned lines. That is, it will be in the position of player and referee at the same time.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: When this act is in operation, would a company, say in British Columbia, whose intention it would be to fly entirely within the province and not outside it, be compelled, before doing so, to come before this board for a licence?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Then I think the committee should be very careful about this bill, because the experience we have had in British Columbia, in coming to Ottawa before the railway board, or before any board here, has not been at all happy. As far as I am concerned, I shall view the bill with some concern if every local operator has to come to Ottawa, before going into business in the province, to seek permission from a board here.
Aeronautics Act

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I cannot understand how the minister will operate under the act after it has been, amended. The purpose of the amendment is to graft on to the Aeronautics Act an air transport board which I understand the Minister of Munitions and Supply will operate, or at least it will operate in conjunction with the Department of Munitions and Supply. He says that the Aeronautics Act will not be amended in any other particular.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: When did I say that? I do not think I did say it.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The question was asked and that, I understood, was the answer. Are there to be other amendments to the Aeronautics Act?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I clearly understood the minister to say that this was the only one.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: No. I said that the act would be amended to make effective the government's policy with regard to civil aviation as announced in the house some time ago. It is being amended in a number of particulars.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Then the description of the minister is one that will be altered?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: You cannot leave the Minister of National Defence at the head of this act if it is the Minister of Munitions and Supply who will operate the board.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The Minister of Transport is the minister named in the act; but, as I explained, the present is a temporary situation which may or may not last for long; only so long as the air services branch of the Department of Transport is administered by the Minister of Munitions and Supply.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Will the air transport board have authority over air service abroad?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Yes, to an extent. I should not like to answer that question with too great finality. It will certainly have jurisdiction over services in Canada. I presume it may not have jurisdiction over Canadian services everywhere.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: A route from Canada to Great Britain, for instance?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: What supervision would it have over that?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
It probably would have the whole supervision. It is difficult to anticipate

what the rules of international air transport will be, but to-day, as between Canada and the United States, this board will have jurisdiction over all lines that are Canadian operations between the two countries. For instance, the line from Toronto to La Guardia field would be under the air transport board.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Would it have supervision over a United States line coming to Canada?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: No. The whole matter is subject to international agreement.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: On the question of international agreement, now that the British have announced that they cannot follow the Canadian plan, is the government proceeding on the basis of making bilateral agreements with other nations?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: With Russia, for example? What is the position? Is our air policy indefinite temporarily?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Everyone's policy is indefinite in that there is no comprehensive international agreement at the moment. Every country in the world is attempting to convince other countries that its owm view of the international situation is the correct view. In consequence of a number of conversations, each view is more or less solidifying toward a common basis that all countries can accept. But until a basis can be found that all countries can accept there will be no international agreement.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: In what direction is it solidifying?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I cannot say exactly. I am not a prophet.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: The minister has paid a high compliment to the United States civil aviation board. I understand there is a radical difference between the policy in the United States and the policy proposed by the minister, in that the United States policy is that there shall be competition over the same routes, whereas in Canada the policy announced by the minister in this house last month was that there should be no competition, or that Trans-Canada Air Lines should have the exclusive right to east and west air lines in Canada and that as regards the feeder lines, such as they were, the individual company should have the exclusive right. I understand that the United States policy is that direct competition is allowed in the major air lines.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
The air system of the United States was developed on just the opposite line,

Farm Credit
the line that competition between air lines should be held to a minimum. The country has been divided into certain areas. For example, American Air Lines has the southern part of the United States, United Air Lines the *central zone, and other air lines the northern zone. Competition has been kept to a minimum. Recently the civil aeronautics authority has announced that it will permit competition on heavily travelled lines. There has been some discussion of allowing competition on the line between New York and Boston, which is a very heavily travelled line. This policy may be carried farther, but this is a new development of the last year or so. Before that, the policy of the board, as I understand it, was to avoid competition over the same route for different carriers. Important centres must necessarily be competitive. Of the four transcontinental systems, all must start from New York and several may touch Chicago. But, generally speaking, there is the least possible duplication of routes between different operations. I might point out that the population of the United States is twelve times as great as that of Canada, and that the area to be covered in the United States and in Canada is about the same. There may come a time when there is sufficient concentration of traffic over Canadian lines to warrant competition, and when that day comes I am sure the government of the day will recognize the fact. At the moment, the chances of survival of a modern and efficient Canadian air line depend, in my opinion, on not having competition of services over the same route.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: But the rates will be regulated?

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I understand one can travel from New York to Chicago by four different lines.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
Yes, but that is only competition between two great travel centres. Those four lines from New.York to Chicago travel different routes, and there are no other cities in between that are served by more than one line.

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to encourage the provision of intermediate term and short term credit to farmers for the improvement and development of farms through bank loans, guaranteed with limitations, by the crown; moneys payable under the act including expenses of administration to ibe paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
I think I had better make
a statement on this resolution, so that the house will have it before it when it considers the bill. If it is convenient I would suggest that discussion be deferred until the bill is before it, because discussion can be carried on much more intelligently if hon. members have the bill before them. But I should make a statement now because it will assist in understanding the bill.
During my statement on second reading of the Bank Act bill I gave a general outline of the purpose and structure of the proposed Farm Improvement Loan Act. As I then said, this measure is in effect collateral to the Bank Act. The amendments to section 88 of the Bank Act will enable the banks to make loans to farmers for the equipping and improvement of their farms and farm homes and to take appropriate security. The Farm Improvement Loans Act is intended to ensure that these newly created credit facilities will be made available to farmers to the fullest possible extent, at reasonable rates of interest and for sufficiently long terms.
This will be accomplished by guaranteeing each bank against loss up to ten per cent of the aggregate amount of loans made by it in accordance with the prescribed conditions. As I have already pointed out, this technique has already been applied with conspicuous success. Under the Home Improvement Loans Act, the banks loaned $50,000,000 mainly to urban home owners, within the period from November, 1936, to October, 1940. In the main these were loans that wrould not otherwise have been made, and it is generally acknowledged that the act made a notable contribution in terms of employment and community welfare. Under that act the banks were guaranteed against loss up to fifteen per cent of the aggregate value of the loans. Actually the losses to date are only three-quarters of one per cent. Conditions may have been especially favourable to repayment as the business cycle was on the upswing
360S
Farm Credit

throughout the period of operations under the home improvement plan, but I think we are justified in concluding that a guarantee of fifteen per cent is unnecessarily high, even for loans to farmers which may be somewhat more risky than loans to urban home owners. Guarantees were also extended to the banks in connection with loans made for the summer stocking of fuel by consumers, and again the lending experience was excellent. All 1943 loans are now paid and only one bad debt had to be written off from 1942.
It is considered that a guarantee of ten per cent of the aggregate amount of loans made by one bank will be sufficient to offset the special risks attaching to farm improvement loans, yet will not be so large as to result in reckless lending without regard to the prospect of repayment. The amount of the guarantee is not, of course, the only factor that will influence the volume of loans. The attitude of the banks is important, and I have reason to believe that they will welcome the opportunity to extend their field of usefulness to farmefs. The experience under the home improvement plan and the coal guarantee scheme must have brought home to many bank managers the opportunities that lie close at hand for serving the needs of individual borrowers.
It is necessary, of course, to fix some limit on the amount of loans to which the ten per cent guarantee applies. Further, we think it is desirable that there should be an opportunity after the scheme has been working for a reasonable period for parliament to review its operations and make whatever changes then seem desirable. For these reasons, it is proposed that the guarantee should be effective in respect of a maximum of $250 million of loans made within a period of three years. Apart from this over-all limitation on the government's liability, there will be provision for termination of the guarantee after due notice on loans in any particular category or made by any particular bank. This will ensure effective control over lending operations.
While the banks will be free to make whatever loans they see fit, at their own risk, under the extended provisions of section 88 of the Bank Act, only loans which comply with certain prescribed conditions as to purpose, eligibility of the borrower, amount of the loan, rate of interest, terms of repayment and security will be eligible for guarantee. In the bill itself the more general conditions will be set forth. Of necessity the details must be left to regulation, just as was done under the home improvement plan.

First, as to purpose: the object of the scheme is to provide the credit needed by farmers to increase the efficiency of their farming operations and to enable them to make their farm homes more comfortable and attractive. With this in view, it is proposed that the guarantee should apply to loans made for the purchase of farm implements and farm equipment, for rural electrification, for the purchase of live stock, for fencing and drainage, for the repair, alteration and construction of farm buildings and for other farm improvement purposes that may later be specified in the regulations. The categories are very broad and include nearly every kind of permanent improvement to a farm or farm home.
The question of eligibility for loans raises-some difficult points on which. there may be differences of opinion. It will be proposed that the benefits of the guarantee should extended to occupiers of farms whose principal occupation consists of farming, and should not be available to landlords or to what might be called gentleman farmers, living on farms but working in the city. I think this is the right principle, but I would be glad to consider the views of the banking and commerce committee if they reach a different conclusion when they come to consider the bill founded on this resolution.
As to the amount of the loan, the scheme is meant to benefit the ordinary farmer and not the big scale operator who can presumably arrange a line of credit without government guarantee. Hence, it is proposed that the guarantee should not be effective in respect of loans to an individual farmer exceeding $3,000. The rate of interest is to be limited to a maximum of five per cent simple interest per annum, which is considerably less than rates generally obtaining for this kind of accommodation to farmers from merchants, dealers or other present sources and is, I believe, somewhat less than the average rate charged to farmers by banks on short-term loans. It is reasonable that the rate should be lower since an important part of the risk is being borne by the government. Nevertheless, earnings must be sufficient to cover the banks' costs of operation and to give them an incentive to go out after business.
Ideally, the terms and methods of repayment should be adapted to the circumstances of the individual farmer, taking into account the purpose and size of the loan. Thus a loan for a permanent improvement, such as a new barn, should in general be amortized over a longer period than a loan for a farm implement, and a loan for a cream separator might well be paid out of the monthly cream cheque, whereas payments on a binder would usually be most

Farm Credit
convenient at harvest time. Quite obviously, the necessary flexibility cannot be achieved by legislation or even by regulation. In the final analysis each loan is an individual personal problem. An attempt will be made, however, to issue certain general instructions for the guidance of bank managers and, as experience is gained, to make these gradually more explicit. In the bill itself the only limitation as to terms of repayment will be that a guaranteed loan must be repayable in full in not more than ten years. In practice most loans will be of much shorter duration, the outside limit being approached only in the case of large loans for the construction of a permanent improvement such as the principal farm dwelling.
With respect to the taking of security for farm improvement loans, it is proposed to require the banks to take the kind1 of security available to them under the Bank Act, except in the case of larger loans for permanent improvements for which special provision will be made in the bill founded on this resolution. Thus a loan for the purchase of a binder will be secured1 by a charge on the binder itself, and a loan for the installation of a farm electric system by a charge on both the movable and affixed parts of that system.
I would also remind the house that the banks have powers to take additional security of any kind after the loan has been made; for instance, if the borrower appears likely to default or has already defaulted.
For ordinary loans for permanent improvements, it is not the intention to require the banks in the first instance to take security on the farm itself even though the value of the property has been enhanced by reason of the improvements made. This decision was reached after very careful consideration, and I am sure it will result in a much freer use of the facilities than if the banks had been required to take a mortgage on the farm for every single loan in this category. Where the loan is for a relatively large amount, repayable over an extended period, however, it is reasonable and prudent to take security on the property which benefits by the expenditure of the loan. The bill will therefore contain a provision giving the banks power to take a mortgage or hypothec upon the farm or an assignment of the rights and interest of a purchaser under an agreement for sale as security for a farm improvement loan exceeding 82,000 and repayable in more than five years.
When the scheme is in operation the great majority of farmers will be _able to arrange a loan at the bank and pay cash to the manufacturer or dealer for his machinery and
equipment. The lower rate of interest payable on farm improvement loans will constitute a direct saving to the farmer, and I am also hopeful that this method of financing will make a real contribution to a reduction in prices of farm implements and equipment. Nevertheless, there is danger that some dealers and manufacturers, now that the risk of loss and the cost of collection are being transferred to the banks and the government, may tend to oversell. This is a thorny problem, and the government intends to initiate discussions with the leading companies at once so that suitable agreements can be worked out in advance of the commencement of the act.
These are the principal provisions of the measure founded on this resolution. I do not think it is necessary for me to deal at length with the reasons which led the government to adopt this particular method of providing intermediate agricultural credit. I stated them in my explanation of the banking legislation on May 2, and I amplified them in closing the debate on second reading of the Bank Act on May 11. Briefly, the reasons are these: this method avoids delay; it avoids the hazards and costs and problems of personnel involved in building up a new organization which would be necessary if we were to establish a new agricultural bank; it avoids duplicating the network of branch banks already in existence; it affords a desirable combination of government assistance with business judgment.
It is interesting to observe that the subcommittee on agricultural policy of the advisory committee on reconstruction, headed by Donald G. McKenzie of Winnipeg, in its final report recommended:
That the dominion government make a careful survey of the schemes for providing short-term and intermediate credit now in force in other countries, with a view to making provision for adequate credit at low rates of interest to deserving farmers, using as far as possible existing facilities, including the chartered banks of Canada.

speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to send this bill to the banking and commerce committee and, if so, at what stage?

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS

Another bill was sent to the banking and commerce committee before the principle was decided on second reading, and I wondered whether the government would think well of dealing with this bill in the same way.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
We are not in committee, but if I may be permitted to say a word I can see the difference perfectly well. However, this measure will open a very wide field of business to the chartered banks, which they have not been able to enter in the past; and although the minister says he understands the chartered banks are favourable to this proposal, I think it would be most valuable to hear the evidence of the chartered banks in that regard, possibly before the principle is decided upon by this house.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: Does this measure extend these facilities just to the ten chartered banks, or to any other financial houses as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: I think it is just to the ten chartered banks. The reason I say "I think" is that there may be other than chartered banks in the province of Quebec, but I do not think so.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: But not to loan companies of any description?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext:
Are the facilities
created by this act to be extended to all kinds of farmers; fruit farmers, dairy farmers and farmers of all types throughout the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: "A farmer" is defined in the bill. I do not like to pick up this draft bill and start quoting from it now; there will be plenty of opportunity for that in the banking and commerce committee.

subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: But not before that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LIMITED GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS FOR IMPROVEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF FARMS
speechtext: No. It is intended that afarmer shall mean a person who is in possession of a farm, and whose principal occupation consists of farming such farm. Then "a farm" is defined to mean land used for the purpose of farming, which term includes live stock raising, dairying, fruit growing and all tillage of the soil.
